A demonstrative case study using a superconducting resonator highlights the capability of this technique to generate thermal images on time scales significantly shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed, thus enabling dynamic thermal characterization with high spatial fidelity. The proposed technique of low-temperature time-resolved scanning laser microscopy offers unique opportunities to explore superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures, and other low-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multiharmonic lock-in detection method using inverse Fast Fourier Transform to reconstruct time-resolved thermal susceptibility images with high spatial resolution. Implemented on a custom scanning laser microscope for low-temperature operation, the technique enables dynamic thermal characterization faster than the intrinsic scanning speed, demonstrated on a superconducting resonator.
AI.motivation: There is a need for dynamic thermal characterization of low-temperature devices (superconductors, 2D materials, planar hybrids) at high spatial resolution, but conventional scanning methods are limited by intrinsically slow scanning speeds that prevent capturing time-evolving thermal behavior.
AI.method: The approach combines a multiharmonic lock-in detection scheme with inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to reconstruct the temporal evolution of thermal susceptibility. The system is built on a custom, modular scanning laser microscope adapted for low working-distance optical cryostats and calibrated for spatial accuracy.
AI.result: A demonstrative case study on a superconducting resonator shows the technique can generate thermal images on time scales significantly shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed, enabling high-fidelity dynamic thermal characterization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed low-temperature time-resolved scanning laser microscopy provides a powerful tool for dynamic thermal studies of superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures, and other low-dimensional systems.

title: Accurate and Transferable Intermolecular Potential Based on Machine-Learned Molecular Electron Density
summary: Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) contain many learnable parameters and therefore require large training datasets. This poses a challenge for developing highly accurate, general-purpose MLFFs because generating high-quality ab initio reference data is computationally expensive. Classical empirical potentials offer a potentially inexpensive source of synthetic training data, but existing models often lack the accuracy needed to provide useful reference energies. Here, we introduce the density-based intermolecular potential (DensIP), a physics-based model of intermolecular interactions that uses machine-learned electron densities and only four universal parameters. We train and test DensIP on CCSD(T)/CBS interaction energies from DES15K, a dataset of dimers of small organic molecules. DensIP achieves sub-kcal/mol errors for dimers containing molecules absent from the training set, including molecules in non-equilibrium conformations, demonstrating strong transferability. We further show that DensIP can be applied to molecules as large as drug ligands. Notably, DensIP outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions, making it a promising approach for generating accurate synthetic training data at scale.

AI.tldr: DensIP is a physics-based intermolecular interaction model using machine-learned electron densities with only four universal parameters, achieving sub-kcal/mol accuracy on CCSD(T)/CBS interaction energies for small organic molecule dimers, outperforming general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions and offering a scalable source of synthetic training data.
AI.motivation: MLFFs require large training datasets, but generating high-quality ab initio reference data is computationally expensive. Classical empirical potentials could provide inexpensive synthetic data, but lack the accuracy needed for useful reference energies.
AI.method: DensIP is a density-based intermolecular potential that uses machine-learned electron densities and only four universal parameters. It is trained and tested on CCSD(T)/CBS interaction energies from the DES15K dataset, which contains dimers of small organic molecules.
AI.result: DensIP achieves sub-kcal/mol errors for dimers containing molecules absent from the training set, including non-equilibrium conformations, demonstrating strong transferability. It extends to molecules as large as drug ligands and outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions.
AI.conclusion: DensIP is a promising approach for generating accurate synthetic training data at scale for developing highly accurate general-purpose MLFFs.

title: Graphon Spin Systems as Exactly Solvable Models
summary:
Graphons are measurable functions used to describe the asymptotic behavior of convergent graph families. Originally motivated by problems in combinatorics and graph theory, graphons have found numerous applications in the modeling and analysis of dynamical processes on networks.
  In this work, we use graphons to formulate the Ising model on convergent graph sequences, which include many network topologies common in applications. We derive the mean-field limit for the resulting model and obtain exact results for phase transitions in such systems. Specifically, we show that the critical temperatures of the Ising model on graphons are determined by the eigenvalues of the Hilbert-Schmidt operator associated with the graph limit. For many important network topologies, these eigenvalues can be computed explicitly.
  We illustrate our results with three representative random network models: Erdős-Rényi, small-world, and power-law. In the small-world case, we demonstrate phase transitions to both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases, as well as coexistence of local minima of the free energy. The latter gives rise to multistability, as confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations.
  The results of this work demonstrate that the Ising model on graphons combines the analytical tractability of exactly solvable mean-field models with the ability to accommodate a broad range of network topologies. We expect that the use of graphons in spin models will lead to new insights into the statistical physics of interacting systems on complex networks.

AI.tldr: This paper uses graphons to formulate and solve the Ising model on convergent graph sequences. The critical temperatures are determined by eigenvalues of the Hilbert-Schmidt operator associated with the graph limit. Results are illustrated on Erdős-Rényi, small-world, and power-law networks, with the small-world case showing ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic phase transitions and free-energy multistability confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: While graphons have been widely used to describe the asymptotic behavior of convergent graph families in combinatorics and dynamical processes on networks, their application to spin models—specifically the Ising model—provides a way to bridge analytical tractability of mean-field models with a broad range of realistic network topologies.
AI.method: The authors formulate the Ising model on graphons via convergent graph sequences, derive the mean-field limit of the resulting model, and show that critical temperatures are determined by the eigenvalues of the Hilbert-Schmidt operator associated with the graph limit. Exact results for phase transitions are obtained, with eigenvalues computed explicitly for representative network topologies.
AI.result: For the small-world network case, phase transitions to both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases are demonstrated, along with coexistence of local minima of the free energy leading to multistability. All findings are validated by Monte Carlo simulations. Erdős-Rényi and power-law models are also analyzed.
AI.conclusion: The Ising model on graphons combines the analytical tractability of exactly solvable mean-field models with the flexibility to accommodate diverse network topologies, and this approach is expected to yield new insights into statistical physics of interacting systems on complex networks.

title: Neural quantum states in condensed matter: advances, best practices, and prospects
summary: Neural quantum states provide flexible variational representations of quantum many-body wave functions by combining neural-network parametrizations with Monte Carlo sampling. In this perspective, we review recent advances in their application to condensed-matter systems, focusing on frustrated quantum magnets, interacting lattice fermions, and non-equilibrium dynamics. We discuss the architectures, symmetry constraints, optimization methods, and sampling strategies underlying state-of-the-art calculations, and summarize practical guidelines for reliable simulations. We also examine the principal remaining challenges, including learning non-trivial sign and phase structures, controlling variational bias, enforcing physical symmetries, scaling optimization to large networks, and achieving stable real-time evolution. Finally, we outline promising directions in which neural quantum states may extend the reach of classical simulations of strongly correlated quantum matter.

AI.tldr: This perspective reviews recent advances in neural quantum states (NQS)—variational quantum many-body wave functions combining neural-network parametrizations with Monte Carlo sampling—applied to condensed-matter systems, focusing on frustrated magnets, interacting fermions, and non-equilibrium dynamics. It covers architectures, symmetry constraints, optimization methods, sampling strategies, practical guidelines, remaining challenges, and future directions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide a comprehensive perspective on the rapidly evolving field of neural quantum states, summarizing the state of the art in their application to strongly correlated quantum matter and identifying key challenges and promising directions for extending classical simulation capabilities.
AI.method: The paper is a perspective/review that synthesizes recent advances in NQS, covering (1) network architectures and symmetry constraints, (2) optimization methods and Monte Carlo sampling strategies, (3) practical guidelines for reliable simulations, and (4) an analysis of outstanding challenges including sign/phase structure learning, variational bias control, symmetry enforcement, large-network scaling, and real-time evolution stability.
AI.result: The paper identifies the principal remaining challenges for NQS: learning non-trivial sign and phase structures, controlling variational bias, enforcing physical symmetries, scaling optimization to large networks, and achieving stable real-time evolution. It also outlines promising directions to extend classical simulations of strongly correlated quantum matter.
AI.conclusion: Neural quantum states hold significant promise for extending the reach of classical simulations of strongly correlated quantum systems, with well-defined technical challenges ahead that, if addressed, could unlock broader applicability across frustrated magnets, interacting fermions, and non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Planar Nanofluidic Memristors Enabled by Surface Charge Gradient
comment: Main text: 7 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material: 17 pages, 13 figures
summary: Nanofluidic memristors, exploiting ion transport in nanochannels, hold promise for neuromorphic applications. A planar architecture is particularly desired for scalable integration with established micro- and nanofabrication technologies. Here, using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck framework, we theoretically propose planar nanofluidic memristors enabled by surface charge gradient, providing an alternative to the commonly used geometrically asymmetric architectures. The resulting memristive behavior is governed by a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect. By systematically solving the PNP equations, we obtain the scaling of the characteristic memory time across the parameter space. We also reveal that the memory effect is related to the first-order moment of surface charge, for arbitrary charge profiles. These results provide a theoretical basis for rationally designing and optimizing planar nanofluidic memristors through spatially patterned surface charge.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically proposes planar nanofluidic memristors enabled by surface charge gradients, using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck framework, as an alternative to geometrically asymmetric architectures. The memristive behavior arises from a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect, with memory time scaling characterized across parameter space and the memory effect linked to the first-order moment of surface charge.
AI.motivation: Nanofluidic memristors are promising for neuromorphic applications, but existing designs rely on geometrically asymmetric architectures. A planar architecture is desired for scalable integration with established micro- and nanofabrication technologies, motivating the search for an alternative mechanism.
AI.method: The authors employ the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) framework to theoretically design planar nanofluidic memristors. They systematically solve the PNP equations to obtain scaling of the characteristic memory time across parameter space and derive a relationship between the memory effect and the first-order moment of surface charge for arbitrary charge profiles.
AI.result: The study reveals that planar memristive behavior is governed by a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect. The memory time scaling is characterized across the parameter space, and it is shown that the memory effect is related to the first-order moment of surface charge for arbitrary charge profiles.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a theoretical basis for rationally designing and optimizing planar nanofluidic memristors through spatially patterned surface charge, offering a scalable alternative to geometrically asymmetric architectures.

title: Doping-driven Mott transition from steady-state density functional theory
summary: The doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model is described within the frame- work of steady-state density functional theory, or i-DFT. In order to access the many-body spectral function in i-DFT, an approximation for the exchange-correlation (xc) bias at arbitrary density and current is required. By using Fermi-liquid theory, a connection between the xc bias of i-DFT and the quasiparticle weight of many-body theory is derived and the results are employed to guide the construction of the approximation. Numerical results obtained with this functional demonstrate that the doping-driven Mott transition can indeed be captured with i-DFT.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a density functional theory approach (i-DFT) combined with Fermi-liquid theory to capture the doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model, deriving a connection between the exchange-correlation bias and quasiparticle weight to construct an accurate functional.
AI.motivation: To extend steady-state density functional theory (i-DFT) to capture the many-body spectral function of the Hubbard model, which requires an accurate approximation for the exchange-correlation (xc) bias at arbitrary density and current.
AI.method: The authors use Fermi-liquid theory to derive a relationship between the xc bias in i-DFT and the quasiparticle weight of many-body theory, using this connection to guide the construction of a new approximation for the xc functional.
AI.result: Numerical results obtained with the constructed functional demonstrate that the doping-driven Mott transition can indeed be captured within the i-DFT framework.
AI.conclusion: i-DFT, when augmented with a Fermi-liquid-theory-informed xc approximation, is a viable framework for describing the doping-driven Mott transition in strongly correlated electron systems.

title: Interplay of nonrelativistic and relativistic spin splittings in altermagnets
summary: Despite their compensated magnetic moments, altermagnets (AMs) exhibit nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) that offers routes to spintronic functionality without relying on relativistic spin-orbit coupling. However, how NRSS influences relativistic phenomena remains largely unexplored. Here we show that NRSS plays a crucial role in reshaping the Rashba effect in AMs with broken inversion symmetry. Using a tight-binding model, we demonstrate that Rashba spin splitting, whose magnitude is typically limited by the strength of spin-orbit coupling, is governed by NRSS energy scales. The resulting Rashba bands combined with NRSS generate anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with a Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization. First-principles calculations for the noncentrosymmetric AM GdAlSi corroborate the emergence of these effects in a real system. Our results reveal the interplay between nonrelativistic and relativistic effects in AMs and identify them as fertile platforms for spin-orbitronic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) in altermagnets with broken inversion symmetry plays a crucial role in reshaping the Rashba effect, enabling anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization, as corroborated by first-principles calculations on GdAlSi.
AI.motivation: Although altermagnets exhibit nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) that offers spintronic functionality without relativistic spin-orbit coupling, how NRSS influences relativistic phenomena (such as the Rashba effect) remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors employ a tight-binding model to demonstrate that Rashba spin splitting is governed by NRSS energy scales rather than being limited solely by spin-orbit coupling strength. They further perform first-principles calculations for the noncentrosymmetric altermagnet GdAlSi to confirm the emergence of these effects in a real material.
AI.result: Rashba spin splitting is reshaped by NRSS, and the resulting Rashba bands combined with NRSS produce anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with a Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization. First-principles calculations on GdAlSi corroborate these effects.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal the interplay between nonrelativistic and relativistic effects in altermagnets and identify them as fertile platforms for spin-orbitronic applications.

title: Superconducting ground state study of Cr-based equiatomic high-entropy alloy through $μ\text{SR}$
summary: High-entropy alloy superconductors, characterized by extreme chemical disorder and complex electronic environments, have attracted significant attention as model systems for exploring superconductivity in disordered materials. Here, we investigate a Cr-based equiatomic HEA, Cr-V-Ti-Nb-Ta, which contains a magnetic 3d element, providing an opportunity to examine the influence of magnetic elements on superconductivity in highly disordered systems. Despite expected magnetic pair-breaking, this alloy exhibits bulk type-II superconductivity with a transition temperature of $T_c = 2.33(3)$ K and a high upper critical field. Transverse-field $μ$SR measurements reveal an s-wave superconducting gap close to the BCS value, while zero-field $μ$SR suggests preserved time-reversal symmetry. These results establish Cr-V-Ti-Nb-Ta as a promising platform for exploring the interplay between disorder, magnetism and superconductivity in high entropy alloys.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a Cr-based high-entropy alloy superconductor, Cr-V-Ti-Nb-Ta, which contains a magnetic 3d element. Despite expected magnetic pair-breaking, the alloy exhibits bulk type-II superconductivity with Tc = 2.33 K, a high upper critical field, an s-wave superconducting gap close to the BCS value, and preserved time-reversal symmetry. It is established as a platform for studying the interplay between disorder, magnetism, and superconductivity in HEAs.
AI.motivation: To examine the influence of magnetic elements on superconductivity in highly disordered high-entropy alloy systems, using a Cr-based equiatomic HEA containing a magnetic 3d element as a model system.
AI.method: The study employs bulk electrical transport/magnetization measurements to establish superconductivity (Tc = 2.33 K and upper critical field), combined with transverse-field muon spin rotation (μSR) to probe the superconducting gap symmetry, and zero-field μSR to examine time-reversal symmetry breaking.
AI.result: The Cr-V-Ti-Nb-Ta alloy exhibits bulk type-II superconductivity despite the presence of magnetic Cr. The superconducting gap is s-wave and close to the BCS value, and time-reversal symmetry is preserved. The upper critical field is high.
AI.conclusion: Cr-V-Ti-Nb-Ta represents a promising material platform for exploring the interplay between disorder, magnetism, and superconductivity in high-entropy alloys.

title: Towards Ultra Scalability of Non-Volatile Magnetic Tunnel Junctions with a 3D Storage Layer
summary: The perpendicular Spin Transfer Torque Magnetic Random Access Memory is one of the most promising emerging non-volatile memory technologies, based on ultra-thin magnetic tunnel junctions. However, as these devices are limited by their thermal stability factor at technological nodes smaller than 20 nm, their scalability is compromised. A possible solution to this limitation relies on taking advantage of the shape anisotropy, by increasing substantially the thickness of the storage layer. Thanks to the combination of a vertical aspect-ratio and enhanced volume, high thermal stability can be maintained at sub-10 nm nodes. Here, we present the technological advancements and understanding of the magnetisation reversal that led to faster switching speeds at reduced switching voltage, providing a viable approach for dense arrays of ultra-small magnetic tunnel junctions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a solution to the thermal stability limitation of perpendicular STT-MRAM devices at sub-20nm nodes by increasing the storage layer thickness to leverage shape anisotropy, maintaining high thermal stability at sub-10nm nodes while achieving faster switching speeds at reduced switching voltages.
AI.motivation: Perpendicular STT-MRAM is a promising emerging non-volatile memory technology, but its scalability is compromised at technology nodes smaller than 20nm due to limitations in the thermal stability factor of ultra-thin magnetic tunnel junctions.
AI.method: The approach increases the thickness of the storage layer substantially to exploit shape anisotropy, combining a vertical aspect-ratio with enhanced volume to maintain high thermal stability at sub-10nm nodes.
AI.result: The combination of shape anisotropy and enhanced volume preserves thermal stability at ultra-small nodes while enabling faster switching speeds at reduced switching voltages, providing a viable approach for dense arrays of ultra-small magnetic tunnel junctions.
AI.conclusion: Thicker storage layers leveraging shape anisotropy offer a practical path to overcome the thermal stability-scaling tradeoff in perpendicular STT-MRAM, enabling scalability to sub-10nm technology nodes.

title: Orbital-Optimized Quasi-Variational Distinguishable Cluster Doubles Method
summary: We present the orbital-optimized quasi-variational distinguishable cluster doubles (OQVDCD) method, obtained by applying the distinguishable cluster (DC) approximation to orbital-optimized quasi-variational coupled cluster doubles (OQVCCD). The resulting method retains a Hermitian-like energy functional, is size-extensive, obeys the generalized Hellmann-Feynman theorem at a stationary point, is exact in the isolated two-electron and two-hole limits, and scales as O(o2v4), like coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD). For the tested closed-shell reaction energies, it is shown that OQVDCD reduces the mean absolute deviation relative to OQVCCD from 1.20 to 0.81 kcal/mol, bringing the errors close to distinguishable cluster singles and doubles (DCSD). In the strongly correlated examples considered here, OQVDCD shifts the OQVCCD energies toward the benchmark, although the convergence remains somewhat less robust than for DCSD.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OQVDCD, an orbital-optimized quasi-variational distinguishable cluster doubles method that combines the DC approximation with OQVCCD. It is size-extensive, Hermitian-like, obeys the Hellmann-Feynman theorem, is exact in two-electron/two-hole limits, and scales as O(o2v4). It improves reaction energy accuracy over OQVCCD (MAD reduced from 1.20 to 0.81 kcal/mol) and performs better in strongly correlated systems, though convergence is somewhat less robust than DCSD.
AI.motivation: To develop a computational electronic structure method that improves upon OQVCCD in terms of accuracy for both closed-shell reaction energies and strongly correlated systems, while retaining favorable properties like size-extensivity and manageable computational scaling.
AI.method: OQVDCD is derived by applying the distinguishable cluster (DC) approximation to orbital-optimized quasi-variational coupled cluster doubles (OQVCCD). The method maintains a Hermitian-like energy functional and is implemented with O(o2v4) scaling, comparable to CCSD.
AI.result: OQVDCD reduces the mean absolute deviation of reaction energies relative to OQVCCD from 1.20 to 0.81 kcal/mol, approaching DCSD-level accuracy. In strongly correlated systems, OQVDCD shifts OQVCCD energies toward benchmark values, though its convergence robustness is somewhat inferior to DCSD.
AI.conclusion: OQVDCD is a promising method that offers improved accuracy over OQVCCD while sharing favorable properties such as size-extensivity, a variational-like energy functional, and reduced computational cost relative to higher-order methods, making it a useful alternative for both weakly and strongly correlated electronic structure problems.

title: Conservation capacity of local learning rules in physical networks
summary: How many memories can a local learning rule protect, and what fixes the number? Physical learning rules train resistive networks through local measurements, and the standard rules conserve a mass-like function of the conductances, a law whose general form was posed as an open problem with the expectation that no useful solution theory exists. We answer it, in the direction the expectation ran against, and the answer is a capacity theory. The Tellegen identity behind the conserved mass localizes: the feedback state is pinned to zero at the inputs, so every sector of the circuit that the input electrodes separate carries its own private conserved mass, by an argument consuming only Kirchhoff's law and that boundary condition, hence valid for arbitrary nonlinear branch laws. The number of independent sector masses is a topological property of the circuit, bounded by the number of output electrodes. An untrainable element can destroy the mass of its own sector and of no other, which says where fixed nonlinear components may be placed; per-edge learning rates select which functionals are conserved and never how many; and adjoint coupled learning, which clamps its outputs before measuring, drains every output-carrying sector at a rate set by the squared output multipliers. In linear circuits we then classify the identities: exact rational computation over all 502 circuits on up to five vertices with two inputs and one or two outputs, and hundreds of larger ones, yields a closed-form count, proved on that family and conjectured in general, with the sector statement a theorem at every circuit size. The anticipated series-parallel polynomial laws appear as exactly the series-class cubic differences, and the number the opening question asks for is a budget: one designed mass per sector, the differences the topology donates, and one broadcast scalar for each protected functional beyond.

AI.tldr: This paper solves the open problem of the general form of conserved mass functions in local physical learning rules for resistive networks, discovering that the Tellegen identity localizes per sector of the circuit separated by input electrodes. The number of conservable sector masses is a topological property bounded by the number of output electrodes. The paper provides exact rational classification over all 502 circuits up to five vertices, proving a closed-form count for that family and conjecturing it generally, framing the answer as a capacity theory.
AI.motivation: Standard physical learning rules conserve mass-like functions of conductances, but the general form of this conservation law was posed as an open problem with expectations that no useful solution theory exists. The authors aim to answer this question and establish a capacity theory for how many memories can be protected by local learning rules.
AI.method: The authors leverage the Tellegen identity to show that the feedback state is pinned to zero at inputs, implying every sector separated by input electrodes carries its own private conserved mass, using only Kirchhoff's law and boundary conditions (valid for arbitrary nonlinear branch laws). They classify identities in linear circuits via exact rational computation over all 502 circuits on up to five vertices with two inputs and one or two outputs, plus hundreds of larger circuits, yielding a closed-form count.
AI.result: The number of independent sector masses is a topological circuit property bounded by the number of output electrodes. Untrainable elements destroy only their own sector's mass; per-edge learning rates select which functionals are conserved but not how many; adjoint coupled learning drains output-carrying sectors at a rate set by squared output multipliers. A closed-form count is proved for up-to-five-vertex circuits and conjectured generally, with the sector statement a theorem at all circuit sizes.
AI.conclusion: The conserved mass law's general form exists and yields a capacity theory: one designed mass per sector, differences donated by topology, and one broadcast scalar per protected functional beyond. This answers the open problem in the direction opposite to prior expectations and provides a principled account of memory capacity in local learning rules.

title: Phase control of magnon-phonon coupling via magnetic field
summary: We study the phase of the coupling between magnons and surface acoustic wave (SAW) phonons in magnetic thin films. The coupling constant changes from a real to a complex number as the external magnetic field is reduced. Below a transition field, the imaginary coupling constant allows SAW phonons to couple to overdamped magnons whose resonance frequency is close to zero and far from the SAW resonance. The strength of the imaginary coupling constant and the magnitude of the transition field both scale with magnetic damping. We find the coupling produces a broad, pronounced minimum in the SAW transmittance spectrum near zero magnetic field in a Ni/Ru/Ni synthetic antiferromagnet with large magnetic damping. These results demonstrate that the phase of the complex magnon-phonon coupling constant can be tuned via magnetic field in strongly damped magnets, offering a platform to explore novel regimes of magnon-phonon interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the phase of magnon-SAW phonon coupling in magnetic thin films, showing that the coupling constant transitions from real to complex as the external magnetic field is reduced. In strongly damped magnets like a Ni/Ru/Ni synthetic antiferromagnet, the imaginary coupling enables coupling to overdamped magnons, producing a broad transmittance minimum near zero field. The imaginary coupling strength and transition field both scale with magnetic damping, demonstrating that the complex coupling phase can be tuned via magnetic field.
AI.motivation: To understand how the phase (real vs. imaginary) of the magnon-phonon coupling constant evolves with magnetic field and how this affects SAW transmittance, particularly in strongly damped magnetic systems where novel coupling regimes may emerge.
AI.method: The study analyzes the magnetic field dependence of the magnon-SAW phonon coupling constant in magnetic thin films, examining how the coupling transitions from real to complex below a critical field. It uses a Ni/Ru/Ni synthetic antiferromagnet with large magnetic damping and measures the SAW transmittance spectrum as a function of magnetic field.
AI.result: The coupling constant changes from real to complex below a transition field, allowing SAW phonons to couple to overdamped magnons with near-zero resonance frequency far from the SAW resonance. The imaginary coupling strength and transition field both scale with magnetic damping. A broad, pronounced transmittance minimum near zero field is observed in the Ni/Ru/Ni synthetic antiferromagnet.
AI.conclusion: The phase of the complex magnon-phonon coupling constant can be tuned via external magnetic field in strongly damped magnets, offering a platform to explore new regimes of magnon-phonon interactions that are inaccessible in weakly damped systems.

title: Berry-Curvature Effect in Anomalous Transport
summary: A theory of the Berry-phase effect in anomalous transport in ferromagnets driven by statistical forces such as the gradient of temperature or chemical potential has been developed by Di Xiao et al in Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 026603 (2006) based on a field-dependent density of states generating an additional contribution to the current density. We present an alternative derivation of the Berry- phase effect in anomalous transport in altermagnets and noncentrosymmertric metals based on quasiclassic matrix kinetic equation. Along with anomalous Hall effect an anomalous heat flow and anomalous thermalelectric currents are also derived.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an alternative derivation of the Berry-phase effect in anomalous transport in altermagnets and noncentrosymmetric metals using a quasiclassic matrix kinetic equation, deriving anomalous Hall, heat flow, and thermoelectric currents.
AI.motivation: To provide an alternative theoretical framework for the Berry-phase effect in anomalous transport, complementing the existing approach by Di Xiao et al. based on field-dependent density of states.
AI.method: The authors use a quasiclassic matrix kinetic equation approach to derive the Berry-phase contributions to anomalous transport in altermagnets and noncentrosymmetric metals.
AI.result: Along with the anomalous Hall effect, the derivation yields anomalous heat flow and anomalous thermoelectric currents in these materials.
AI.conclusion: The alternative derivation reproduces and extends Berry-phase transport effects beyond the standard density-of-states-based formulation, covering altermagnets and noncentrosymmetric metals.

title: Aging Phase Diagram and Exact Asymptotic Energies of Mixed Spherical Spin Glasses
summary: We determine the aging phase diagram of mixed spherical $(p+s)$-spin glasses quenched from random configurations to zero temperature. Solving the asymptotic dynamical equations of Cugliandolo and Kurchan, we find transitions between aging states with one, two, and continuously many effective temperatures, including phases in which discrete and continuous hierarchies coexist. We obtain analytic expressions for the energies reached asymptotically by the dynamics. In models combining pairwise and higher-order interactions, and sufficiently separated interaction orders ($s>3$), a fully continuous phase exists, where the gradient descent relaxation converges to the algorithmic energy lower bound. Instead, in mixed models with only high-order interactions ($p\ge3$) the energy relaxation remains strictly above it. Numerical integration of the dynamical equations is consistent with the predicted two-step and mixed discrete--continuous aging states.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the zero-temperature aging phase diagram of mixed spherical (p+s)-spin glasses quenched from random configurations. Using Cugliandolo-Kurchan asymptotic dynamical equations, it finds transitions between aging states with one, two, and infinitely many effective temperatures, including coexisting discrete and continuous hierarchies. Analytic expressions for asymptotic energies are derived, showing that models with pairwise and higher-order interactions (s>3) can reach the algorithmic energy lower bound via fully continuous gradient descent, while pure high-order models (p≥3) remain strictly above it.
AI.motivation: To characterize the full aging phase diagram of mixed spherical spin glasses at zero temperature, and to understand how the structure of interaction orders determines the complexity of aging states (number of effective temperatures and hierarchy types) and the asymptotic energy relaxation behavior.
AI.method: Solving the asymptotic dynamical equations of Cugliandolo and Kurchan for mixed spherical (p+s)-spin glasses quenched from random initial configurations to zero temperature. The analysis involves classifying aging states based on the number of effective temperatures (one, two, or continuous) and their possible coexistence, complemented by numerical integration of the dynamical equations.
AI.result: Transitions are found between aging states with one, two, and continuously many effective temperatures, including phases where discrete and continuous hierarchies coexist. Analytic expressions for asymptotic energies are derived. For models with pairwise and higher-order interactions with sufficiently separated orders (s>3), a fully continuous phase exists where gradient descent reaches the algorithmic energy lower bound. In mixed models with only high-order interactions (p≥3), the energy relaxation stays strictly above this bound. Numerical integration confirms the predicted two-step and mixed discrete-continuous aging states.
AI.conclusion: The aging dynamics of mixed spherical spin glasses exhibit rich phase structure governed by the interaction-order composition. The presence of well-separated low-order interactions enables the system to achieve optimal algorithmic energy relaxation through continuous aging hierarchies, whereas purely high-order models are intrinsically constrained to remain above the energy lower bound.

title: AutoMOOSE: Use Case and Logical Views of Agentic Phase-Field Simulation Software
summary: AutoMOOSE is an agentic software framework that converts a natural-language request into an executed, screened, and interpreted MOOSE phase-field simulation. Here, we deploy AutoMOOSE as a agentic software, complementing our prior work which focused on development of the agentic tool. We describe our software framework and architecture through Use Case and logical views of the 1+5 architectural-views model, covering its user roles, component structure, six-agent pipeline, physics plugin layer, Model Context Protocol interface, and screening/falsification/recovery loop. Our architecture separates physical falsification from automatic repair, so corrected simulations remain inspectable and must be re-admitted before acceptance. We focus on software design, extensibility, interoperability, and reuse of the AutoMoose framework for broad utilization in multiphysics materials design problems.

AI.tldr: AutoMOOSE is an agentic software framework that converts natural-language requests into executed, screened, and interpreted MOOSE phase-field simulations, described here through Use Case and logical architectural views.
AI.motivation: To extend prior work on the AutoMOOSE agentic tool by deploying it as a full software framework, emphasizing software design, extensibility, interoperability, and reuse for multiphysics materials design problems.
AI.method: The framework is described via the 1+5 architectural-views model, covering user roles, component structure, a six-agent pipeline, a physics plugin layer, a Model Context Protocol interface, and a screening/falsification/recovery loop. Architecture separates physical falsification from automatic repair so corrected simulations must be re-admitted before acceptance.
AI.result: A deployable agentic software framework that converts natural language to screened and interpreted MOOSE phase-field simulations, with an architecture ensuring corrected simulations remain inspectable through a falsification-repair-readmission workflow.
AI.conclusion: AutoMOOSE provides a robust, extensible architecture for automating multiphysics materials simulations, with clear separation of concerns between physical validation and automatic repair to maintain inspectability and trust.

title: A differentiable photon-by-photon likelihood for continuous free-energy landscapes and diffusion coefficients from single-molecule FRET
summary: Single-molecule FRET probes the conformational dynamics of biomolecules by measuring the distance between two dyes. The experiment produces a stream of coloured photons, which is only an indirect readout of these dynamics. Recovering the free-energy landscape and diffusion coefficient from such a photon stream is a difficult inverse problem. Existing approaches assume a small number of discrete states, bin the photons, or are computationally expensive. Here we derive an exact likelihood for the recorded photon stream under a model in which the dye distance diffuses on a continuous free-energy landscape. It uses the raw inter-photon times and colours at full time resolution, and analytically integrates out all hidden trajectories. The likelihood is differentiable, so automatic differentiation returns exact gradients with respect to all model parameters. This lets us jointly infer the free-energy landscape, the diffusion coefficient, and the photophysical parameters by gradient-based optimization. On simulated data, we recover free-energy landscapes, including ones with a short-lived intermediate, together with the diffusion coefficients. Uncertainties follow from the curvature of the likelihood, computed directly from the same gradients. The framework also guides experimental design. Before any data are recorded, we can evaluate how much a given acquisition setting reduces the resulting uncertainty. Evaluation on the GPU is fast, and independent traces are processed in parallel, so a single fit converges in minutes and scales to large datasets. The likelihood extends photon-by-photon analysis to continuous free-energy landscapes and diffusion coefficients, putting fast quantitative inference with uncertainties within reach of the smFRET community.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact, differentiable likelihood for single-molecule FRET photon streams under a continuous free-energy landscape diffusion model, enabling gradient-based joint inference of free-energy landscapes, diffusion coefficients, and photophysical parameters at full time resolution, with GPU-accelerated parallel processing and uncertainty estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing smFRET analysis methods assume discrete states, bin photons (losing time resolution), or are computationally expensive. Recovering continuous free-energy landscapes and diffusion coefficients from raw photon streams is a difficult inverse problem that current approaches cannot efficiently solve.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact likelihood for the recorded photon stream under a model where the dye distance diffuses on a continuous free-energy landscape. The likelihood uses raw inter-photon times and colors at full time resolution, analytically integrates out all hidden trajectories, and is differentiable so automatic differentiation provides exact gradients for gradient-based optimization of all model parameters simultaneously.
AI.result: On simulated data, the method recovers free-energy landscapes (including those with short-lived intermediates) and diffusion coefficients. Uncertainties are obtained from the curvature of the likelihood computed from the same gradients. The framework also guides experimental design by predicting how acquisition settings reduce uncertainty before data collection. GPU evaluation is fast, processes independent traces in parallel, and converges in minutes even for large datasets.
AI.conclusion: The likelihood extends photon-by-photon analysis to continuous free-energy landscapes and diffusion coefficients, making fast quantitative inference with uncertainties accessible to the smFRET community.

title: Emergent Vibronic Spectral Hierarchy in a Kagome Flat-Band Insulator
summary: Electron-phonon coupling is usually understood in terms of electronic quasiparticles interacting with dispersive lattice vibrations. Much less is known about the complementary limit in which the relevant phonon mode is itself localized or weakly dispersive. Here we investigate this regime in the kagome compound Rb$_{2}$Ni$_{3}$S$_{4}$, which undergoes an unconventional insulating transition near $T^{*} \approx$ 260-280~K. Combining polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy with temperature-dependent x-ray diffraction, scanning tunneling microscopy, and electrical, thermal, and magnetic measurements, we show that the transition involves electronic localization without a conventional structural or magnetic order parameter. Raman spectra reveal a giant Franck-Condon progression associated with a nearly dispersionless 333.7~cm$^{-1}$ phonon, decorated by an equally spaced comb-like fine structure with a characteristic spacing of 40.6~cm$^{-1}$. The comb spacing is insensitive to magnetic field, whereas its spectral weight is strongly field tunable. Rather than treating either hierarchy alone as pure phonon effect, we interpret their nested coexistence as evidence for a strongly coupled electron-vibrational manifold involving a localized lattice coordinate. These results identify dispersionless phonons as an active route to vibronic correlations in solids and suggest that such electron-vibrational self-trapping is closely associated with the insulating phase of Rb$_{2}$Ni$_{3}$S$_{4}$.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the kagome compound Rb₂Ni₃S₄, which undergoes an unconventional insulating transition near 260–280 K. Combining multiple experimental techniques, the authors discover a giant Franck-Condon progression from a nearly dispersionless 333.7 cm⁻¹ phonon decorated by a 40.6 cm⁻¹ comb-like fine structure. They interpret this nested structure as evidence for strong electron-vibrational coupling involving a localized lattice coordinate, identifying dispersionless phonons as a route to vibronic correlations in solids.
AI.motivation: While electron-phonon coupling is well understood for dispersive lattice vibrations interacting with electronic quasiparticles, the complementary limit—where the phonon mode is localized or weakly dispersive—remains poorly understood. This work aims to investigate this regime experimentally.
AI.method: The authors combine polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy with temperature-dependent x-ray diffraction, scanning tunneling microscopy, and electrical, thermal, and magnetic measurements to characterize the insulating transition in Rb₂Ni₃S₄.
AI.result: The transition involves electronic localization without a conventional structural or magnetic order parameter. Raman spectra show a giant Franck-Condon progression from a nearly dispersionless 333.7 cm⁻¹ phonon, decorated by an equally spaced comb-like fine structure with 40.6 cm⁻¹ spacing. The comb spacing is magnetic-field insensitive, but its spectral weight is strongly field tunable.
AI.conclusion: The nested coexistence of these two hierarchies is interpreted as evidence for a strongly coupled electron-vibrational manifold involving a localized lattice coordinate, suggesting that dispersionless phonons provide an active route to vibronic correlations and electron-vibrational self-trapping in solids, closely associated with the insulating phase.

title: Machine Learning Guided Discovery of Corundum High Entropy Oxides
summary: Early thinking in the field of high entropy oxides (HEOs) emphasized their likely abundance, with combinatorial arguments hinting at a myriad of new materials. The experimental reality has proven more challenging: the stability of HEOs cannot be straightforwardly predicted based on ionic radii, lattice geometry, and charge-balancing considerations alone. In this work, we employ machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to predict the synthesizability of HEOs of the form $A_2$O$_3$ derived from a selection of trivalent cations. From nearly 500 possible compositions, we identify 16 promising candidates for experimental validation with solid-state and combustion synthesis. We discover three new HEOs in the corundum structure, including (Al,Cr,Fe,Rh,Sc)$_2$O$_3$, and one novel cation-ordered phase, (Al,Fe,Ga,Sc)$_2$O$_3$. By far the most common synthesis outcome was a mixture of competing phases, sometimes involving redox reactions. Our results also reveal profound synthesis method dependence for the final product, where qualitatively equivalent outcomes between the two synthesis methods were only observed for 3 of the 16 tested compositions. We conclude that the occurrence rate of HEOs is far rarer than initially believed and that machine learning approaches can effectively guide us to the "needle in the haystack".

AI.tldr: This paper uses machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to predict synthesizable high entropy oxides (HEOs) of the form A₂O₃ from ~500 trivalent cation compositions, identifying 16 candidates for experimental validation. Three new corundum HEOs and one cation-ordered phase were discovered, but most compositions phase-separated, revealing that HEOs are far rarer than initially believed and that synthesis method dramatically affects outcomes.
AI.motivation: Early theoretical arguments suggested HEOs should be abundant, but experimental reality shows their stability cannot be predicted from simple ionic radii, lattice geometry, or charge-balancing rules alone. This discrepancy motivates the need for more sophisticated predictive tools to efficiently guide experimental discovery.
AI.method: The authors employ machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to screen ~500 possible A₂O₃ compositions derived from trivalent cations. The 16 most promising candidates were selected and validated experimentally using solid-state and combustion synthesis methods.
AI.result: Three new HEOs in the corundum structure were discovered, including (Al,Cr,Fe,Rh,Sc)₂O₃, plus one novel cation-ordered phase (Al,Fe,Ga,Sc)₂O₃. The most common outcome was mixtures of competing phases, sometimes involving redox reactions. Only 3 of 16 tested compositions gave qualitatively equivalent results across both synthesis methods, indicating profound synthesis method dependence.
AI.conclusion: HEOs are far rarer than initially believed, and machine learning approaches (specifically MLIPs) can effectively guide researchers to the rare synthesizable compositions—the "needle in the haystack"—highlighting the value of computational screening for experimental allocation.

title: Intracavity Photon Statistics from Correlated Molecular Electronic Structure
summary: Quantum optics characterizes light through photon correlations, but ab initio cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) has only calculated raw field moments at present. In this study, intracavity photon statistics of cavity-coupled molecules are computed from QED coupled-cluster (QED-CCSD-22) densities and validated against exact diagonalization of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian. A change of coordinate origin or dipole convention displaces the ground state coherently, so second-order and higher cumulants of the cavity field are well defined even for molecular ions. The photon subsystem of QED Hartree-Fock is exactly coherent, so the invariant statistics measure electron-photon correlation. The field fluctuations are super-Poissonian, and their degree of second-order coherence is set by the cavity frequency rather than by the coupling strength, falling from 18.5 to 4.9 for H2 as the cavity is detuned from 5 to 20 eV. A parity selection rule makes the sign of the third cumulant a probe of the orientation of the molecular charge asymmetry along the cavity polarization.

AI.tldr: This paper computes intracavity photon statistics of cavity-coupled molecules from ab initio QED coupled-cluster (QED-CCSD-22) densities, validated against exact diagonalization. It shows that cumulants of the cavity field beyond first order are well-defined and invariant, and reveals super-Poissonian field fluctuations whose second-order coherence depends on cavity frequency (18.5 to 4.9 for H2 from 5 to 20 eV), with the third cumulant acting as an orientation probe of molecular charge asymmetry via a parity selection rule.
AI.motivation: Quantum optics describes light via photon correlations, but ab initio cavity QED has so far only computed raw field moments. This work aims to bridge this gap by computing higher-order photon statistics (cumulants) directly from QED densities.
AI.method: Intracavity photon statistics are computed from QED coupled-cluster densities (specifically QED-CCSD-22) and validated against exact diagonalization of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian. Cumulant analysis is used, noting that a change of coordinate origin or dipole convention coherently displaces the ground state, making second-order and higher cumulants well-defined even for molecular ions. QED Hartree-Fock is shown to produce an exactly coherent photon subsystem, so the invariant statistics serve as a measure of electron-photon correlation.
AI.result: The cavity field fluctuations are super-Poissonian. The degree of second-order coherence is governed by the cavity frequency rather than the coupling strength, decreasing from 18.5 to 4.9 for H2 as the cavity is detuned from 5 to 20 eV. A parity selection rule determines that the sign of the third cumulant probes the orientation of the molecular charge asymmetry along the cavity polarization.
AI.conclusion: Ab initio QED methods can now go beyond raw field moments to provide genuine photon correlation statistics. The super-Poissonian nature and frequency-dependent coherence of cavity fields are revealed, and the third-order cumulant offers a new observable for diagnosing molecular orientation and charge asymmetry in strongly coupled cavity systems.

title: The Trachenko-Zaccone equation: nonlinear relaxation from glasses to complex systems
summary: The Trachenko-Zaccone equation provides a compact nonlinear dynamical framework for describing non-Debye relaxation in disordered condensed matter. Originally developed to rationalize stretched- and compressed-exponential relaxation in liquids and glasses from the dynamics of interacting local relaxation events, the same equation has subsequently appeared in broader contexts, including polymer relaxation and nonlinear models of global population dynamics. This review retraces the conceptual development of the equation, with particular emphasis on its physical origin in Kostya Trachenko's feed-forward interaction mechanism, its mathematical structure, and its possible generalizations. We also include personal recollections of the work with Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London in August 2019, during which the equation emerged in essentially its present form. After reviewing applications to stress relaxation, glassy materials, polymer relaxation and population dynamics, we discuss future directions including time-dependent feedback parameters, coupled order parameters, heterogeneous and spatially resolved formulations, flux terms, network versions and stochastic extensions. The central theme of the review is that the Trachenko-Zaccone equation should be viewed not only as a model of glassy relaxation, but as a general nonlinear feedback equation with potential applications across complex systems.

AI.tldr: This is a review paper tracing the conceptual development, mathematical structure, and applications of the Trachenko-Zaccone equation, a compact nonlinear dynamical framework originally developed for non-Debye relaxation in glasses and liquids but applicable more broadly to polymer relaxation and population dynamics. The review highlights its physical origin in Trachenko's feed-forward interaction mechanism, documents its emergence in 2019, surveys applications across multiple fields, and outlines future directions including time-dependent feedback, coupled order parameters, heterogeneous formulations, flux terms, network versions, and stochastic extensions. The central thesis is that this equation should be viewed as a general nonlinear feedback equation with broad relevance to complex systems.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive review of the Trachenko-Zaccone equation, documenting its conceptual development, physical foundations, mathematical structure, applications across disparate fields, and future research directions, with the broader goal of establishing it as a general nonlinear feedback framework applicable to complex systems beyond glassy relaxation.
AI.method: This is a review article that retraces the conceptual development of the equation, analyzes its mathematical structure and generalizations, includes personal recollections of its formulation at Queen Mary University of London in August 2019, surveys applications in stress relaxation, glassy materials, polymer relaxation, and population dynamics, and discusses prospective extensions such as time-dependent feedback parameters, coupled order parameters, heterogeneous formulations, flux terms, network versions, and stochastic extensions.
AI.result: The review consolidates the Trachenko-Zaccone equation as a unifying nonlinear feedback framework that has successfully described stretched- and compressed-exponential relaxation in liquids, glasses, polymers, and even population dynamics, and identifies multiple concrete future directions for generalization and broader application across complex systems.
AI.conclusion: The Trachenko-Zaccone equation should be recognized not merely as a model of glassy relaxation but as a general nonlinear feedback equation with potential applicability across diverse complex systems, opening avenues for further generalization and interdisciplinary use.

title: Long-lived Laughlin pairs in a depleted quantum Hall edge channel
summary: On-demand sources and mesoscopic beam splitters allow individual ballistic electrons to collide in depleted quantum Hall edge channels, where their unscreened Coulomb interaction acts as a strong, controllable nonlinearity. Theory suggests a more striking possibility: in a strong magnetic field, the repulsion can drive quantized relative circulation, allowing two electrons to propagate together as a positive-energy Laughlin pair. The relevance of such pairs to experiment depends on quantitative lifetimes in realistic guiding potentials and on whether the proposed collision pathway to pair formation survives full two-dimensional dynamics. We develop a microscopic theory of quasibound Laughlin pairs using the physical two-electron Hamiltonian. For a general local electric-field gradient, we determine the dissociation threshold, number of quasibound states, and decay rates. Complex scaling and analytic tunneling theory show that lifetimes grow exponentially with pair energy above threshold. Applied to reported GaAs parameters, the theory indicates that existing devices may already support the lowest spin-polarized pair, with a leading lifetime estimate about three orders of magnitude longer than typical propagation times. We simulate a collision with the full finite-field Hamiltonian, demonstrating both a framework for nonlinear two-electron quantum dynamics and the creation of a Laughlin pair in a representative two-electron collision. We use Husimi distributions and their zeros to visualize both quasibound resonances and transient collision states in phase space. These results place the preparation, propagation, and detection of repulsively paired electrons within reach of existing single-electron circuit technology. They identify kinematic stabilization under constrained one-dimensional propagation as a pairing mechanism that may extend to anyonic quantum Hall edge excitations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a microscopic theory of quasibound Laughlin pairs in quantum Hall edge channels, showing that two repulsively interacting electrons can form bound positive-energy pairs with exponentially growing lifetimes. Applied to GaAs parameters, existing devices may support pair lifetimes ~3 orders of magnitude longer than propagation times, and full two-dimensional collision simulations demonstrate the formation of Laughlin pairs via nonlinear electron dynamics.
AI.motivation: Theory suggests that in strong magnetic fields, Coulomb repulsion between ballistic electrons in quantum Hall edge channels could drive quantized relative circulation, forming positive-energy Laughlin pairs. However, the experimental relevance of such pairs depends on quantitative lifetimes in realistic potentials and whether the proposed collision pathway survives full 2D dynamics—questions that had not been resolved.
AI.method: The paper uses a physical two-electron Hamiltonian to develop a microscopic theory of quasibound Laughlin pairs. For a general local electric-field gradient, they determine dissociation thresholds, number of quasibound states, and decay rates using complex scaling and analytic tunneling theory. They simulate collisions with the full finite-field Hamiltonian and use Husimi distributions with zeros to visualize quasibound resonances and transient collision states in phase space.
