Applied to GaAs parameters, existing devices may already support the lowest spin-polarized pair, with lifetime estimates roughly three orders of magnitude longer than typical propagation times. Full collision simulations demonstrate the creation of a Laughlin pair in representative two-electron collisions, establishing a framework for nonlinear two-electron quantum dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The preparation, propagation, and detection of repulsively paired electrons are within reach of existing single-electron circuit technology. The work identifies kinematic stabilization under constrained one-dimensional propagation as a pairing mechanism that may extend to anyonic quantum Hall edge excitations.

title: Two distinct gap structures in the mid-infrared optical conductivity of the Hubbard model
summary: Mid-infrared (MIR) optical conductivities in cuprate superconductors show universal features. In this study, we demonstrate that these originate from two distinct gaps: the pseudogap mediated by antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations and the Mott-Hubbard gap. The MIR spectra from these two gaps show a characteristic and distinct shape and doping dependence, and can thus be distinguished. Specifically, the Mott-Hubbard correlations, while rendering a peak in the visible spectrum for small dopings, yield a broad optical response starting in the MIR when a ``waterfall'' develops in the one-particle spectrum at larger dopings. The numerically and analytically determined doping-dependence of both gaps consistently reproduce experiments, and provide a unified microscopic understanding of the cuprate MIR optical conductivity.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that universal mid-infrared (MIR) optical conductivity features in cuprate superconductors originate from two distinct gaps: the pseudogap (mediated by antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations) and the Mott-Hubbard gap. These gaps produce characteristic, distinguishable MIR spectral shapes and doping dependencies, and their numerically and analytically determined doping dependence consistently reproduces experiments, providing a unified microscopic understanding.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of universal MIR optical conductivity features in cuprate superconductors, which had previously lacked a unified microscopic understanding.
AI.method: The study identifies two distinct gaps contributing to MIR spectra—the pseudogap from antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations and the Mott-Hubbard gap—and analyzes their characteristic spectral shapes and doping dependence via numerical and analytical approaches, including how Mott-Hubbard correlations shift from visible-peak behavior at low doping to broad MIR response when a 'waterfall' develops in the one-particle spectrum at higher doping.
AI.result: The numerically and analytically determined doping dependence of both gaps consistently reproduces experimental observations, and the two gaps can be distinguished by their distinct spectral shapes and doping behavior in the MIR regime.
AI.conclusion: The universal MIR optical conductivity in cuprates arises from the combined contributions of the pseudogap and the Mott-Hubbard gap, yielding a unified microscopic description of these optical features.

title: Orbital-Selective Spin Splitting in the Altermagnetic Ti$_2$XX' Monolayers
summary: Altermagnets have attracted intensive attention recently, owing to their unique combination of zero net magnetic moment of antiferromagnets and momentum space spin-splitting of ferromagnets. Herein, we systematically explore monolayer altermagnetic Ti$_2$XX' (X/X' = F, Cl, Br, I) materials for novel electronic properties. Especifically, spin-splitting exists in the valence bands of all studied materials, whereas several compositions exhibit nearly spin-degenerate conduction bands near the Fermi level, which is markedly different from conventional altermagnets. This phenomenon can be attributed to the bond-angle-sensitive super-exchange occurring in the $d_{xz}$ or $d_{yz}$ orbitals, while the super-exchange of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital is not sensitive to the Ti-X-Ti bond angle. Motivated by this intriguing phenomenon, Fermi level modulation via doping or heterostructure construction enables the transition between two electronic states, endowing these materials great application potential in information storage devices.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically explores monolayer altermagnetic Ti2XX' (X/X' = F, Cl, Br, I) materials, discovering spin-splitting in valence bands across all compositions but nearly spin-degenerate conduction bands in several cases—a deviation from conventional altermagnets. This phenomenon arises from bond-angle-sensitive super-exchange in dxz/dyz orbitals versus bond-angle-insensitive super-exchange in dx2-y2 orbitals. Fermi level modulation via doping or heterostructures can enable transitions between electronic states, showing potential for information storage devices.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets are an emerging class of materials combining the zero net magnetic moment of antiferromagnets with the momentum-space spin-splitting of ferromagnets. The authors aim to explore monolayer Ti2XX' materials to discover novel electronic properties and understand the microscopic origin of unconventional spin behaviors in two-dimensional altermagnetic systems.
AI.method: The study systematically investigates monolayer altermagnetic Ti2XX' compounds (X/X' = F, Cl, Br, I) using computational approaches, analyzing their electronic band structures with a focus on spin-splitting behavior. The authors attribute observed phenomena to orbital-specific super-exchange interactions, specifically comparing the bond-angle sensitivity between dxz/dyz and dx2-y2 orbitals in Ti-X-Ti super-exchange pathways. They also propose Fermi level engineering strategies via doping or heterostructure construction.
AI.result: All studied monolayer Ti2XX' materials exhibit spin-splitting in valence bands, but several compositions show nearly spin-degenerate conduction bands near the Fermi level—distinct from conventional altermagnets. This difference is explained by the bond-angle-sensitive super-exchange in dxz/dyz orbitals versus the bond-angle-insensitive super-exchange in the dx2-y2 orbital.
AI.conclusion: Fermi level modulation through doping or heterostructure construction enables switching between the spin-split and spin-degenerate electronic states, making these materials promising candidates for information storage device applications.

title: Machine-Learned NMR Shieldings in Molecular Solids with Built-In Hybrid-Functional Molecular Corrections
summary: Fast and accurate chemical shielding estimators are essential for shielding-driven Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) crystallography. Machine-learning models for shielding predictions have matured significantly and today are primarily limited by the electronic structure reference data they are trained on. Here, we introduce ShiftML4, a shielding-tensor model trained directly on monomer-corrected calculations that approximate PBE0, rather than the PBE reference targeted by earlier ShiftML models. ShiftML4 is trained on a diverse set of structures containing 12 of the most common NMR nuclei in molecular organic solids. On experimental benchmark sets, the 13C isotropic RMSE against experiment is 1.67 ppm, compared with 2.34 ppm for GIPAW-PBE on the same geometries. ShiftML4 gives a similar 1H prediction RMSE to ShiftML3 (0.5 ppm) and improves the 15N RMSE from 7.24 to 6.08 ppm. The model also reduces errors in the shielding-tensor anisotropy, with an RMSE of 4.63 ppm on 13C CSA principal components against 5.85 ppm for GIPAW. The improvements in prediction accuracy are retained on better geometries. Basing shift predictions on structures relaxed with PET-MOLS, a recent machine-learned interatomic potential that reaches approximate hybrid-DFT geometries in seconds, lowers the ShiftML4 errors further to 0.48 ppm (1H), 1.49 ppm (13C) and 3.66 ppm (15N).

AI.tldr: ShiftML4 is a new machine-learning shielding-tensor model trained on monomer-corrected PBE0-approximate calculations, outperforming earlier ShiftML models and GIPAW-PBE across 1H, 13C, and 15N NMR predictions, with further error reduction when combined with PET-MOLS-relaxed geometries.
AI.motivation: Fast and accurate chemical shielding estimators are critical for shielding-driven NMR crystallography. Machine-learning models for shielding prediction are now limited primarily by the quality of the electronic structure reference data they are trained on, motivating the need for a model trained on higher-level (PBE0-approximate) references rather than PBE.
AI.method: ShiftML4 is trained directly on monomer-corrected calculations that approximate PBE0, covering 12 of the most common NMR nuclei in molecular organic solids. The model is evaluated on experimental benchmark sets, and its performance is further tested in combination with PET-MOLS, a machine-learned interatomic potential providing approximate hybrid-DFT geometries.
AI.result: ShiftML4 achieves a 13C isotropic RMSE of 1.67 ppm vs 2.34 ppm for GIPAW-PBE on the same geometries, a 1H RMSE similar to ShiftML3 (0.5 ppm), and improves 15N RMSE from 7.24 to 6.08 ppm. The shielding-tensor anisotropy error also drops, with 13C CSA principal component RMSE of 4.63 ppm vs 5.85 ppm for GIPAW. Combined with PET-MOLS geometries, errors reduce further to 0.48 ppm (1H), 1.49 ppm (13C), and 3.66 ppm (15N).
AI.conclusion: Training on monomer-corrected PBE0-approximate reference data substantially improves shielding prediction accuracy across multiple nuclei and tensor components. The combination of ShiftML4 with PET-MOLS-relaxed geometries yields the best performance, demonstrating the value of pairing high-quality reference data with accurate, fast structure relaxation.

title: Maxwell's Demon in Markov Chain Monte Carlo: Cooling Information Flow and Entropy Balance
summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms can be viewed as feedback devices that compare a proposed move with the target distribution and then accept or reject it. In this paper the Maxwell demon is identified with the acceptance module: it measures a proposed edge, stores the outcome in the accept/reject bit, and uses that bit to shape the probability current. The decision bit carries a genuine Shannon mutual information about the proposal, whereas only its directional part is converted into a cooling information flow. The relative-entropy relaxation rate obeys $v(t)=\dot{\mathcal I}_{\rm cool}(t)+\dot S(t)$, which separates useful cooling from housekeeping circulation in nonreversible chains.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the Maxwell demon in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms with the acceptance module, which measures proposed moves and stores outcomes in accept/reject bits. The decision bit carries Shannon mutual information about the proposal, but only its directional part converts into cooling information flow. The relative-entropy relaxation rate follows v(t) = dI_cool/dt + dS/dt, separating useful cooling from housekeeping circulation in nonreversible chains.
AI.motivation: To provide a thermodynamically grounded interpretation of MCMC algorithms by connecting the acceptance mechanism to Maxwell demon-like information processing, and to decompose the relaxation dynamics into useful cooling versus wasteful circulation components.
AI.method: The paper adopts an information-theoretic and thermodynamic framework, modeling MCMC as a feedback device where the acceptance module acts as a Maxwell demon that measures proposed moves and stores outcomes in a decision bit. It computes Shannon mutual information and information flows, and derives a decomposition of the relative-entropy relaxation rate in terms of cooling information flow and entropy production.
AI.result: The relative-entropy relaxation rate satisfies v(t) = dI_cool/dt + dS(t), providing a clear separation between useful cooling information flow and housekeeping circulation in nonreversible MCMC chains.
AI.conclusion: MCMC acceptance mechanisms can be interpreted as Maxwell demons, and the resulting information-theoretic decomposition offers a new lens for understanding and possibly optimizing the efficiency of sampling algorithms by distinguishing useful cooling from dissipative circulation.

title: Dissipation driven boundary localization in higher order topological insulators
summary: We study dissipation driven boundary localization in a Bernevig Hughes Zhang type second order topological insulator by introducing inhomogeneous, spin dependent boundary dissipation. After projection onto the edge subspace, the dominant component of the boundary dissipation lies in the same Pauli channel as the kinetic term. This channel gives both counter-propagating edge modes the same real transfer exponent. The two modes therefore accumulate at the same dissipative domain wall. For the corner states, the dissipative envelope competes with Jackiw Rebbi localization. Increasing dissipation moves their weight from the geometric corners to the dissipative domain wall. Propagating edge states also localize at this wall. Numerical calculations confirm the qualitative predictions of the edge theory. A fixed energy Feshbach reduction captures finite size effects. Inhomogeneous boundary dissipation thus controls boundary state localization without changing the bulk topology.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how inhomogeneous, spin-dependent boundary dissipation controls localization of boundary states in a Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang type second-order topological insulator. Dissipation causes both counter-propagating edge modes to accumulate at a dissipative domain wall, competing with Jackiw-Rebbi localization for corner states. This boundary dissipation controls localization without altering the bulk topology.
AI.motivation: To understand and control how dissipation-driven boundary localization affects edge and corner states in higher-order topological insulators, specifically whether inhomogeneous boundary dissipation can manipulate boundary state localization without changing the bulk topology.
AI.method: The authors employ edge subspace projection to analyze the dominant Pauli channel of boundary dissipation, derive real transfer exponents for edge modes, use Jackiw-Rebbi analysis for corner states, and perform numerical calculations. A fixed energy Feshbach reduction is used to capture finite size effects.
AI.result: The dominant boundary dissipation component lies in the same Pauli channel as the kinetic term, giving both counter-propagating edge modes the same real transfer exponent, causing them to accumulate at the same dissipative domain wall. Corner state weight shifts from geometric corners to the dissipative domain wall as dissipation increases. Propagating edge states also localize at this wall. Numerical results confirm the edge theory predictions.
AI.conclusion: Inhomogeneous boundary dissipation provides a mechanism to control boundary state localization in second-order topological insulators without altering the bulk topology, offering a new tuning knob for topological boundary states.

title: Magnetic-Field Selection of Magnetic Order in Altermagnets and Noncollinear Antiferromagnets
summary: Conventional field selection of magnetic order relies on the Zeeman coupling, which, however, vanishes in magnets without net magnetization, a rapidly growing class including altermagnets (AMs), noncollinear antiferromagnets (nc-AFMs), and PT-symmetric antiferromagnets (PT-AFMs). Here we show that the quantity that fundamentally couples a magnet to a uniform magnetic field is not the magnetization, but the binary order parameter eta that labels the two time-reversal-related minima of the Landau free energy. We develop a Landau theory of order selection based on eta under the constraints of magnetic point-group (MPG) symmetry, in which eta couples to odd-degree polynomials in the magnetic field. Within this framework, the linear term is the ferromagnetic Zeeman coupling, while higher-order couplings with leading degree n = 3, 5, 7, and 9 naturally appear in AMs and nc-AFMs. In contrast, combined PT symmetry forbids any such coupling. Consequently, it is the order-(n-1) magnetic susceptibility, rather than the net magnetization, that serves as the primary experimental observable for identifying the magnetic order of AMs and nc-AFMs. For all 122 MPGs, we classify the leading coupling degree and the corresponding polynomial forms. We demonstrate our framework in two representative materials: the AM MnF2 and the nc-AFM MnTe2. We further construct a symmetry-allowed spin model for an AM system to reveal the microscopic origin of the higher-order coupling and establish the coupling coefficient explicitly in terms of the spin-model parameters. Our work unifies the description of magnetic-order selection across magnets with and without net magnetization, offers a microscopic origin for this counterintuitive physics, and provides fingerprints for distinguishing intrinsic field selection from extrinsic switching.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a Landau theory showing that the fundamental quantity coupling a magnet to a uniform magnetic field is a binary order parameter labeling two time-reversal-related minima of the free energy, not the magnetization. This allows field selection of magnetic order in magnets without net magnetization (altermagnets, noncollinear antiferromagnets) via higher-order couplings (n=3,5,7,9), while PT-symmetric antiferromagnets forbid such coupling. The order-(n-1) magnetic susceptibility serves as the experimental observable. They classify all 122 magnetic point groups and demonstrate the framework in MnF2 and MnTe2.
AI.motivation: Conventional field selection of magnetic order relies on Zeeman coupling, which vanishes in magnets without net magnetization—a rapidly growing class including altermagnets, noncollinear antiferromagnets, and PT-symmetric antiferromagnets. A framework is needed to understand how magnetic order can be selected by a uniform magnetic field in these systems.
AI.method: The authors develop a Landau theory of order selection based on a binary order parameter η that labels two time-reversal-related minima of the Landau free energy, constrained by magnetic point-group symmetry. η couples to odd-degree polynomials in the magnetic field. They classify the leading coupling degree and polynomial forms for all 122 magnetic point groups, and construct a symmetry-allowed spin model to reveal the microscopic origin of the higher-order coupling.
AI.result: The linear term in the framework corresponds to ferromagnetic Zeeman coupling, while higher-order couplings with leading degree n=3, 5, 7, and 9 naturally appear in altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets. PT symmetry forbids any such coupling. The order-(n-1) magnetic susceptibility is the primary experimental observable. The framework is demonstrated in MnF2 (altermagnet) and MnTe2 (noncollinear antiferromagnet), and the coupling coefficient is established explicitly in terms of spin-model parameters.
AI.conclusion: The work unifies the description of magnetic-order selection across magnets with and without net magnetization, provides a microscopic origin for this counterintuitive physics, and offers fingerprints for distinguishing intrinsic field selection from extrinsic switching.

title: Machine learning predictions of the Hessian matrix for peptides chains and small proteins
summary: Molecular Hessians have a key role in describing molecular vibrations, trajectories and optimization paths. An explicit calculation of them through standard quantum mechanical methods can be computationally expensive for medium-large systems, and in many applications not even needed. Machine learning methods can be a shortcut to tackle efficiently the computational difficulties. This paper will present a ML model able to predict the Hessian matrix of biological system made of thousands of atoms. The method, based on learning the Hessian in internal coordinates is intrinsically invariant to molecular rotations and translations, and has a very good scaling with the systems' size. The training was performed on a dataset of simple aminoacids, as they constitute the building blocks of larger proteins. From the predicted Hessian matrix it is possible to calculate thermochemical properties within the harmonic approximations, among them enthalpies, entropies, Gibbs' free energies, and zero point vibrational energies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a machine learning model that predicts molecular Hessian matrices (second derivatives of energy) for biological systems with thousands of atoms. The model learns Hessians in internal coordinates, making it invariant to rotations and translations, and scales well with system size. Trained on amino acids, it enables calculation of thermochemical properties like enthalpies, entropies, Gibbs free energies, and zero-point vibrational energies within the harmonic approximation.
AI.motivation: Explicit calculation of molecular Hessians via standard quantum mechanical methods is computationally expensive for medium-to-large systems and often unnecessary for many applications. A faster ML-based approach is needed.
AI.method: A machine learning model is trained to predict the Hessian matrix in internal coordinates, ensuring intrinsic invariance to molecular rotations and translations. The model is trained on a dataset of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and demonstrates favorable scaling with system size.
AI.result: The model successfully predicts Hessian matrices for biological systems of thousands of atoms, allowing the computation of thermochemical properties (enthalpies, entropies, Gibbs free energies, zero-point vibrational energies) within the harmonic approximation.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning offers an efficient shortcut to computing molecular Hessians for large biological systems, avoiding expensive quantum mechanical calculations while enabling access to key thermochemical quantities.

title: Interedge backscattering in quantum spin Hall-based NS and SNS junctions
comment: 9+6 pages and 5+7 figures, comments are welcome
summary: We investigate the microscopic conditions that allow for the coupling between opposite quantum spin Hall (QSH) edges in hybrid junctions with superconductors. Using a microscopic Bernevig--Hughes--Zhang model and the Bogoliubov--de Gennes formalism, we model a potential barrier along the NS interface and identify the parameter regimes in which the QSH edges are coupled. In normal--superconductor junctions, such coupling manifests as deviations from the quantized zero-bias Andreev conductance $G=4e^2/h$. These deviations are controlled by the induced gap in the barrier, the barrier geometry, the interface transparency, orbital and Fermi-velocity mismatch, and disorder strength as well as the bias voltage leading to a zero-bias peak. We then analyze the impact of this interedge-coupling mechanism in Josephson junctions at equilibrium and show that it hybridizes the edge-resolved Andreev branches, opens gaps at the time-reversal-invariant phase differences $\varphi=0$ and $\varphi=π$, and modifies the superconducting quantum interference pattern. In a reflection-symmetric geometry, the relative sizes of the two gap openings provide complementary information about the interedge dynamical phase, which also determines the parity of the suppressed lobes in the magnetic interference pattern. This investigation sheds light on the microscopic details that control the coupling of helical edge states in actual devices and the resulting consequences for superconducting hybrid systems.

The authors identify parameter regimes where QSH edges couple in normal-superconductor junctions (manifesting as deviations from quantized Andreev conductance G=4e²/h) and analyze the impact of this interedge coupling on Josephson junctions, showing it hybridizes Andreev branches, opens gaps at φ=0 and φ=π, and modifies superconducting interference patterns.

They systematically vary parameters including induced gap in the barrier, barrier geometry, interface transparency, orbital and Fermi-velocity mismatch, disorder strength, and bias voltage to map out the regimes where QSH edge coupling occurs. In Josephson junctions, interedge coupling hybridizes edge-resolved Andreev branches and opens gaps at time-reversal-invariant phase differences φ=0 and φ=π. title: Ultralow-Field Triplon Condensation in a Spin-Ladder Magnet
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material: 13 pages, 7 figures, 1 table
summary: We realise the first ultralow-field Bose-Einstein condensation of triplons in a spin-ladder magnet, uncovering a quantum critical point at only $μ_0 H_{c1}=0.17$ T in Henmilite ($\mathrm{Ca_2Cu(OH)_4[B(OH)_4]_2}$). Unlike dimer magnets, a ladder retains extended one-dimensional correlations in its gapped parent state, making this limit strongly fluctuation dominated. Thermodynamic, magnetoelastic, $μ$SR, and neutron-diffraction measurements overturn the previous assignment of zero-field antiferromagnetic order, establishing a quantum-disordered coupled-ladder parent state with persistent low-energy dynamics. The weak low-temperature anomaly instead marks a gap-controlled crossover from the correlated ladder regime into the activated quantum-disordered state. These measurements further reveal an exceptionally asymmetric ordered dome extending to $μ_0 H_{c2}\simeq 8.2$ T. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations for the relevant spin Hamiltonian place Henmilite just on the gapped side of the zero-field ladder-ordering instability, naturally accounting for the strong separation between the exchange and residual-gap scales and the tiny critical field. Our findings extend ultralow-field triplon condensation beyond the dimer paradigm and establish Henmilite as a platform for controlled tuning across quantum criticality in a fluctuation-dominated spin ladder.

AI.tldr: First ultralow-field Bose-Einstein condensation of triplons realized in a spin-ladder magnet (Henmilite), with a quantum critical point at only 0.17 T, overturning previous zero-field ordering assignment and establishing a quantum-disordered coupled-ladder parent state supported by multi-technique experiments and QMC simulations.
AI.motivation: To achieve ultralow-field triplon condensation beyond the dimer magnet paradigm, exploiting spin-ladder systems where extended 1D correlations make the gapped parent state strongly fluctuation-dominated.
AI.method: Combined thermodynamic, magnetoelastic, muSR, and neutron-diffraction measurements, complemented by quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the relevant spin Hamiltonian.
AI.result: Identified a quantum critical point at 0.17 T in Henmilite, established a quantum-disordered coupled-ladder parent state with persistent low-energy dynamics, revealed an asymmetric ordered dome extending to ~8.2 T, and located Henmilite just on the gapped side of the zero-field ladder-ordering instability.
AI.conclusion: Extends ultralow-field triplon condensation beyond the dimer paradigm and establishes Henmilite as a platform for controlled tuning across quantum criticality in a fluctuation-dominated spin ladder.

title: Prediction of a layer nonlinear Hall effect in bilayer nonmagnetic or antiferromagnetic systems
summary: Nonlinear Hall effects provide a powerful probe of quantum geometry in solids and enable rectification phenomena beyond the constraints of linear response. In this Letter, we predict a \emph{layer nonlinear Hall effect} (LNHE) in stacked bilayer systems composed of nonmagnetic or antiferromagnetic materials with a vanishing linear Hall conductivity. In such systems, the second- or third-order nonlinear Hall responses are intrinsically layer odd: the contributions from the two constituent layers have equal magnitude but opposite sign, resulting in exact cancellation under layer-exchange symmetry. An out-of-plane electric field $E_z$ can break this symmetry, thereby unveiling the hidden response and converting it into a switchable macroscopic nonlinear Hall signal. Using a minimal $k\!\cdot\!p$ model, we demonstrate that the LNHE can originate from the Berry curvature dipole mechanism. A systematic symmetry analysis of all 80 layer groups further yields a complete classification of the symmetry constraints and stacking configurations that allow for this type of LNHE. Beyond this mechanism, additional symmetry analysis reveals that LNHE may also arise from quantum metric dipole or inversed mass dipole. Remarkably, even in cases where second-order nonlinear Hall responses are symmetry forbidden, a third-order LNHE can still survive in certain stacked bilayer configurations. First-principles calculations on representative bilayers---nonmagnetic 1T$'$-WTe$_2$ and 1T$'$-ReS$_2$---explicitly demonstrate electrically reversible second-order LNHE, in full agreement with our symmetry-based predictions. Overall, our results establish LNHE as a universal phenomenon in a wide range of layered quantum materials and provide a robust route toward electrically tunable nonlinear transport.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts a layer nonlinear Hall effect (LNHE) in stacked bilayer systems of nonmagnetic or antiferromagnetic materials, where the second- or third-order nonlinear Hall responses are intrinsically layer-odd and cancel under layer-exchange symmetry. An out-of-plane electric field can break this symmetry, converting the hidden response into a switchable macroscopic signal. The effect can arise from Berry curvature dipole, quantum metric dipole, or inversed mass dipole mechanisms, with a complete symmetry classification across all 80 layer groups. First-principles calculations on WTe₂ and ReS₂ bilayers confirm electrically reversible second-order LNHE.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear Hall effects probe quantum geometry in solids and enable rectification beyond linear response. The authors seek to uncover a universal mechanism for nonlinear Hall responses in stacked bilayer systems that would otherwise exhibit vanishing linear (and potentially nonlinear) Hall conductivity due to layer-exchange symmetry, and to provide a route toward electrically tunable nonlinear transport.
AI.method: The study employs (1) a minimal k·p model to demonstrate the Berry curvature dipole origin of LNHE, (2) a systematic symmetry analysis of all 80 layer groups to classify symmetry constraints and stacking configurations permitting LNHE, (3) symmetry analysis for alternative mechanisms including quantum metric dipole and inversed mass dipole, and (4) first-principles DFT calculations on 1T'-WTe₂ and 1T'-ReS₂ bilayers to verify the predicted electrically reversible second-order LNHE.
AI.result: Second- and third-order nonlinear Hall responses are found to be intrinsically layer-odd in stacked bilayers, canceling under layer-exchange symmetry. An Ez field breaks this symmetry and unveils the response. The LNHE is shown to arise from Berry curvature dipole, quantum metric dipole, or inversed mass dipole mechanisms. A complete classification across all 80 layer groups identifies allowing stacking configurations. Even where second-order responses are symmetry-forbidden, third-order LNHE can survive. First-principles calculations confirm electrically reversible second-order LNHE in nonmagnetic 1T'-WTe₂ and 1T'-ReS₂ bilayers, in agreement with symmetry predictions.
AI.conclusion: LNHE is established as a universal phenomenon in layered quantum materials, providing a robust route toward electrically tunable nonlinear transport and a sensitive probe of quantum geometry in stacked bilayer systems.

title: Optical conductivity signature of Van Hove singularity in altermagnetic topological systems
summary: We investigate the topological phases, joint density of states (JDOS), optical conductivities, and magneto-optical responses of a two-dimensional $d$-wave altermagnet with spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman splitting. The system hosts Dirac gaps at the high-symmetry points $Γ$, $\textrm{M}$, $\textrm{X}$, and $\textrm{Y}$. We show that the JDOS exhibits kinks at the corresponding Dirac gap frequencies and pronounced peaks at Van Hove singularities, whose positions can be tuned by the altermagnetic order. These features are reflected in the optical conductivities, with complementary signatures in their real and imaginary parts. Particularly, the Van Hove signatures in the transverse optical conductivity disappear in the absence of $d$-wave altermagnetism, revealing an altermagnet-induced optical signature of the Van Hove singularity. Finally, the Faraday and Kerr rotations inherit characteristic features of the optical conductivity. Our results establish optical and magneto-optical spectroscopy as sensitive probes of Dirac gaps and Van Hove singularities in altermagnetic topological systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the topological and optical properties of a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet with spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman splitting, revealing that joint density of states, optical conductivities, and magneto-optical responses (Faraday/Kerr rotations) exhibit characteristic signatures of Dirac gaps and Van Hove singularities, establishing optical spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of altermagnetic topological systems.
AI.motivation: To understand how altermagnetic order manifests in the optical and magneto-optical responses of two-dimensional topological systems, particularly whether Dirac gaps and Van Hove singularities can be detected through spectroscopic measurements, and to identify altermagnet-specific optical signatures.
AI.method: The authors theoretically investigate a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet with spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman splitting. They compute the joint density of states (JDOS), optical conductivities, and magneto-optical responses (Faraday and Kerr rotations), analyzing kinks at Dirac gap frequencies and peaks at Van Hove singularities, including their tunability by the altermagnetic order.
AI.result: The JDOS exhibits kinks at Dirac gap frequencies at high-symmetry points (Γ, M, X, Y) and pronounced peaks at Van Hove singularities tunable by altermagnetic order. These features appear in the optical conductivities with complementary real/imaginary signatures. Critically, the Van Hove signature in the transverse optical conductivity vanishes without d-wave altermagnetism, providing an altermagnet-specific optical fingerprint. Faraday and Kerr rotations inherit these characteristic features.
AI.conclusion: Optical and magneto-optical spectroscopy are demonstrated to be sensitive probes of Dirac gaps and Van Hove singularities in altermagnetic topological systems, with the transverse optical conductivity providing a distinct signature of d-wave altermagnetism.

title: First-principles design of main-group dimer defects in ZnO as candidate quantum defects
summary: Zinc oxide (ZnO), a wide-band-gap semiconductor with mature growth techniques, is a promising host for optically active quantum spins. Yet, optically active quantum defects in ZnO remain largely unexplored. Here, we identify and characterize a family of double substitutional impurities in ZnO, formed by main-group donor-acceptor (DA) pairs, as candidates for optically active quantum defects. Using hybrid density functional theory (DFT), we systematically investigate double substitutional DA complexes and their defect physics, including electronic structure, thermodynamic stability, and optical properties. The proposed defects exhibit isolated defect states, strong spin localization on the acceptor site, and $C_{3v}$ symmetry. Importantly, the electronic structure of the DA pairs is largely determined by the atomic properties of their constituent atoms. We further examine their optical characteristics, including zero-phonon lines (ZPLs), radiative lifetimes, and nonradiative decay to assess their viability as color centers. Notably, among the dimers, (Si$_{Zn}$-B$_O$)$^+$ and (Ge$_{Zn}$-B$_O$)$^+$ exhibit visible optical transitions with sub-microsecond radiative lifetimes and robust charge states against optical ionization, while (Si$_{Zn}$-C$_O$)$^{2+}$ shows the smallest Huang-Rhys factor, approximately 5.6. Our results propose a new family of main-group donor-acceptor defects in ZnO as promising candidates for optically active spin defects.

Among them, (Si_Zn-B_O)^+ and (Ge_Zn-B_O)^+ show visible optical transitions with sub-microsecond radiative lifetimes and robust charge states, while (Si_Zn-C_O)^2+ exhibits the smallest Huang-Rhys factor (~5.6).
AI.motivation: ZnO is a promising host for optically active quantum spins due to its wide band gap and mature growth techniques, yet optically active quantum defects in ZnO remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: Hybrid density functional theory (DFT) is used to systematically investigate double substitutional main-group donor-acceptor (DA) complexes in ZnO, analyzing their electronic structure, thermodynamic stability, optical properties including zero-phonon lines, radiative lifetimes, and nonradiative decay.
AI.result: The defects exhibit isolated defect states, strong spin localization on the acceptor site, and C_3v symmetry. (Si_Zn-B_O)^+ and (Ge_Zn-B_O)^+ show visible optical transitions with sub-microsecond radiative lifetimes and stability against optical ionization, while (Si_Zn-C_O)^2+ has the smallest Huang-Rhys factor of ~5.6.
AI.conclusion: The study proposes main-group donor-acceptor double substitutional defects in ZnO as a promising new family of optically active spin defects for quantum applications.

title: Electric-Field-Induced Second Harmonic Generation at a Reconfigurable LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ Nanojunction
summary: Electrically tunable nonlinear optical responses at the nanoscale remain challenging to achieve because conventional nonlinear materials lack the combination of large susceptibility, nanoscale confinement, and in situ reconfigurability. Here we report electric-field-induced second harmonic (EFISH) generation from a nanoscale tunnel junction defined by conductive atomic force microscope lithography at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface. A conducting channel written at the interface is interrupted by a nanoscale insulating gap, across which applied DC bias produces local electric fields exceeding $10^7$ V/m. The SHG signal is spatially localized at the junction, exhibits a quadratic bias dependence described by $I(2ω) \propto |χ^{(2)}_\mathrm{0} + χ^{(3)} E_\mathrm{DC}|^2$ with no hysteresis, a modulation depth exceeding 380% at $|V_\mathrm{DC}| = 1$ V, and shows a two-lobed input-polarization pattern aligned with the junction axis, consistent with EFISH from a centrosymmetric host. Calibration against a BBO reference crystal gives $|χ^{(3)}| \approx 1\times10^{-19}$ m$^2$/V$^2$ at 6 K. These results establish cAFM-written oxide nanojunctions as a reconfigurable platform for nanoscale nonlinear optics in which the junction geometry sets the symmetry of the response and the large field-induced $χ^{(2)}$ of SrTiO$_3$ provides the optical nonlinearity. Because the nonlinearity is both generated and read out within the same nanoscale gap, the junction operates simultaneously as a subwavelength source and a near-field detector of optical nonlinearity.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates electrically tunable second harmonic generation from nanoscale tunnel junctions at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interface, created by conductive atomic force microscope lithography. The junction produces local DC electric fields exceeding 10^7 V/m, yielding electric-field-induced SHG with a modulation depth exceeding 380% at 1 V, no hysteresis, and a measured χ(3) ≈ 1×10^-19 m²/V² at 6 K. The device operates as both a subwavelength nonlinear optical source and near-field detector within the same nanoscale gap.
AI.motivation: Electrically tunable nonlinear optical responses at the nanoscale are difficult to achieve because conventional nonlinear materials lack the combined properties of large susceptibility, nanoscale confinement, and in situ reconfigurability. This work addresses this gap by exploiting the large field-induced χ(2) of SrTiO3 in nanoscale oxide junctions.
AI.method: The researchers use conductive atomic force microscope (cAFM) lithography to write a conducting channel at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interface, interrupting it with a nanoscale insulating gap. A DC bias across the gap generates local electric fields exceeding 10^7 V/m. They measure the second harmonic signal, its spatial localization, bias dependence, polarization pattern, and calibrate the third-order susceptibility against a BBO reference crystal.
AI.result: The SHG signal is spatially localized at the junction, exhibits quadratic bias dependence I(2ω) ∝ |χ(2)_0 + χ(3)E_DC|² with no hysteresis, shows a modulation depth exceeding 380% at ±1 V, and displays a two-lobed input-polarization pattern aligned with the junction axis. Calibration yields |χ(3)| ≈ 1×10^-19 m²/V² at 6 K.
AI.conclusion: cAFM-written oxide nanojunctions serve as a reconfigurable platform for nanoscale nonlinear optics, where the junction geometry determines the symmetry of the nonlinear response. The device simultaneously functions as a subwavelength source and a near-field detector of optical nonlinearity, since the nonlinearity is both generated and read out within the same nanoscale gap.

title: Quasi-one-dimensional topological band structure and van Hove singularities in monolayer TaIrTe$_4$ from laser $μ$-ARPES
summary: Recent transport experiments reported a quantum spin Hall insulator phase in monolayer 1T-TaIrTe$_4$ gated away from charge neutrality. This phase is not predicted by band structure calculations and has been attributed to an electronic instability induced by strong correlations at a putative van Hove singularity. Here, we investigate the electronic structure of exfoliated monolayer 1T-TaIrTe$_4$ using micro-focus laser angle resolved photoemission. We find a strongly anisotropic band structure susceptible to density wave instabilities. Our data further reveal a saddle point singularity in the density of states. However, we find that the saddle point lies at a density for which transport experiments found no anomalies. Moreover, the quasiparticle line widths suggest weak electron correlations only. This points to a secondary role of van Hove singularities and electron correlations in the transport phase diagram of monolayer 1T-TaIrTe$_4$.

AI.tldr: Using micro-focus laser ARPES, the authors studied the electronic structure of exfoliated monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4 and found a strongly anisotropic band structure with a saddle-point van Hove singularity in the density of states. However, the saddle point occurs at a doping where transport experiments show no anomalies, and the measured quasiparticle linewidths indicate only weak electron correlations, suggesting that van Hove singularities and correlations play only a secondary role in the transport phase diagram of this material.
AI.motivation: A quantum spin Hall insulator phase was experimentally observed in monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4 when gated away from charge neutrality, but this phase is not predicted by band structure calculations. It has been attributed to an electronic instability driven by strong correlations at a putative van Hove singularity. The authors aim to directly probe the electronic structure to test this hypothesis and clarify the origin of the observed transport anomalies.
AI.method: Micro-focus laser angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was performed on exfoliated monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4 to map its band dispersion and density of states, and to extract quasiparticle linewidths as a measure of electron correlation strength.
AI.result: The data reveal a strongly anisotropic band structure susceptible to density wave instabilities, and a saddle point singularity in the density of states is identified. However, the saddle point is located at a carrier density where transport experiments found no anomalies. Additionally, the quasiparticle linewidths indicate only weak electron correlations.
AI.conclusion: The results argue against strong-correlation-driven van Hove singularities being the dominant mechanism behind the transport phase diagram of monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4, assigning such electronic instabilities and correlations only a secondary role.

title: Systematic and accurate anharmonic formation free energies of metastable defects via a constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force framework
summary: Computing the formation free energies of metastable defects at finite temperature remains challenging due to anharmonicity, the multiplicity of basins and the frequent occurrence of migration events. Using the previously introduced constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force method (BABFc), we establish a practical thermodynamic integration framework for computing restricted anharmonic formation free energies associated with individual metastable defect basins. We demonstrate that BABFc can be exploited as a robust, systematic and numerically efficient tool for addressing a long standing bottleneck in atomistic materials science: the finite temperature thermodynamic characterization of metastable defects in complex, highly anharmonic energy landscapes. The proposed workflow requires only a reference local minimum and a confinement strategy and does not rely on defect specific collective variables. It therefore provides a general route to assign well-defined free energies to individual metastable basins, even when these basins are separated by low barriers and embedded in a dense landscape of competing configurations. In this setting, BABFc enables stable, bias corrected free energy estimates with statistical accuracies at the meV/atom level and a very low failure rate, including for systems containing approximately one thousand atoms. We demonstrate this capability through thousands of independent free energy calculations covering hundreds of four-interstitial and four-vacancy configurations in bcc $α$-Fe over a broad temperature range, using both a traditional empirical potential and a data driven force field.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a thermodynamic integration framework based on the constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force method (BABFc) to compute restricted anharmonic formation free energies of individual metastable defect basins at finite temperature. The workflow requires only a reference minimum and confinement strategy, works without defect-specific collective variables, achieves meV/atom accuracy with low failure rates, and is validated on thousands of interstitial and vacancy configurations in bcc α-Fe using both empirical and machine-learned potentials.
AI.motivation: Computing formation free energies of metastable defects at finite temperature is notoriously difficult due to anharmonicity, multiple energy basins, and frequent migration events. This has been a long-standing bottleneck in atomistic materials science for the thermodynamic characterization of metastable defects in complex, highly anharmonic energy landscapes.
AI.method: The authors use the constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force method (BABFc) within a thermodynamic integration framework. The approach requires only a reference local minimum and a confinement strategy, operates without defect-specific collective variables, and employs bias correction to yield stable free energy estimates.
AI.result: The method achieves statistical accuracies at the meV/atom level with a very low failure rate, even for systems of approximately one thousand atoms. Validation involved thousands of independent free energy calculations covering hundreds of four-interstitial and four-vacancy configurations in bcc α-Fe over a broad temperature range, using both a traditional empirical potential and a data-driven force field.
AI.conclusion: BABFc provides a robust, systematic, and numerically efficient general route to assign well-defined free energies to individual metastable basins, even when basins are separated by low barriers and embedded in dense landscapes of competing configurations.

title: An autonomous feedback protocol: responding to temperature and potential changes in energy converters
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: Nanoscale thermoelectric devices convert tiny amounts of heat into power. But what happens if the external conditions and resulting temperature differences are not a priori known? We propose a feedback mechanism that optimizes the performance of a quantum-point-contact-based heat engine (QPC). A quantum-dot detector measures the external conditions and gives autonomous feedback on the QPC's properties. We expect this feedback mechanism to be experimentally relevant for steady-state engines with unknown external conditions and for adapting dynamic charging processes to the potential buildup.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a feedback mechanism using a quantum-dot detector to autonomously optimize the performance of a quantum-point-contact-based thermoelectric heat engine when external conditions (temperature differences) are unknown or varying.
AI.motivation: Nanoscale thermoelectric devices convert heat into power, but their performance depends on external conditions and resulting temperature differences that may not be known a priori, limiting their practical applicability in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: A quantum-dot detector is used to measure the external conditions and provide autonomous feedback to adjust the properties of a quantum-point-contact-based heat engine (QPC), enabling self-optimization without prior knowledge of the environment.
AI.result: The feedback mechanism is expected to be experimentally relevant for steady-state engines operating under unknown external conditions and for adapting dynamic charging processes to potential buildup.
AI.conclusion: The proposed autonomous feedback mechanism offers a practical solution for optimizing nanoscale thermoelectric engine performance in unknown or dynamically changing conditions, with experimental relevance.

title: Broken Inversion Symmetry via a Magic Methyl Effect
summary: Polar liquid crystals - fluid phases in which molecular dipoles organise into ferro- or antiferroelectric states - present a highly constrained molecular design space, where small changes can entirely suppress polar organisation. Here we demonstrate, contrary to expectations, that installation of a methyl group in the 5-position of a 1,3-dioxane ring substantially increases the onset temperature of polar order. Remarkably, this effect proves transferable across several liquid-crystal families, including examples where the methylated derivative exhibits a polar phase whereas its parent compound does not. Across 8 matched pairs, we find that a 5-methyl group can enhance the onset temperature of polar order in 1,3-dioxane materials by up to 120 °C. These findings establish a simple and general molecular design strategy for enhancing and enabling spontaneous dipolar ordering in liquid crystals.

AI.tldr: Installing a methyl group at the 5-position of a 1,3-dioxane ring significantly increases (by up to 120 °C) the onset temperature of polar order in liquid crystals, a strategy that is transferable across multiple liquid-crystal families and can even enable polar phases in compounds that otherwise lack them.
AI.motivation: Polar liquid crystals have a highly constrained molecular design space where minor structural changes can suppress polar organization, making it difficult to design materials with ferroelectric or antiferroelectric states. Finding a simple, general strategy to enhance polar ordering is needed.
AI.method: Systematic comparison across 8 matched pairs of 1,3-dioxane-based liquid crystals, with and without a 5-methyl substituent, measuring the onset temperature of polar order across several liquid-crystal families.
AI.result: The 5-methyl group enhances the onset temperature of polar order by up to 120 °C, and this effect is transferable across multiple liquid-crystal families, including cases where methylated derivatives exhibit polar phases while parent compounds do not.
AI.conclusion: A 5-methyl substituent on the 1,3-dioxane ring provides a simple, general molecular design strategy for enhancing and enabling spontaneous dipolar ordering in liquid crystals.

title: Continuously control of polarization via electrically driven long-distance superlubric sliding
summary: Sliding ferroelectricity widely exists in various van der Waals bilayers or multilayers, which is induced by asymmetric stacking of commensurate interface. The greatly reduced switching barriers via interlayer sliding lead to high speed with low energy cost, while they are still much higher compared with superlubric sliding of incommensurate interfaces. The polarizations of such incommensurate interfaces are not switchable, which is the major obstacle of combing superlubricity and sliding ferroelectricity for ultralow barriers. Here we propose a design of such combination based on previous synthesis of lateral heterojunctions of 2D materials, which can be extensively applicable to various systems including PN junctions. In such long-distance superlubric ferroelectricity, the vertical polarization can be continuously controlled by superlubric sliding of incommensurate interfaces between lateral heterojunction bilayers, where the series of multiple stable states are long-sought for artificial synaptic devices. The unconventionality of our findings does not only include unprecedented barriers down to the magnitude of mu-eV, but also unprecedented long ion displacements distinct from the small deviations in classical paradigm of ferroelectricity. Our predicted superlubric sliding electrically driven by low vertical voltage is also hitherto reported, much more efficient compared with previously reported sliding mechanically driven by tips, resolving a major issue for practical applications.

AI.method: The authors propose leveraging lateral heterojunctions of 2D materials to create long-distance superlubric ferroelectricity, where superlubric sliding of incommensurate interfaces between lateral heterojunction bilayers enables continuous control of vertical polarization and multiple stable states.

title: Scalable Cyclic Olefin Copolymer Encapsulation for High Optical Quality of TMD Monolayers
summary: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) combine a direct bandgap, strongly bound excitons, and pronounced second-order optical nonlinearity, which makes them promising materials for ultrathin optoelectronic and nanophotonic devices. However, their optical performance is often degraded by environmental exposure and substrate-induced charge trapping, motivating the development of scalable encapsulation strategies. Here, we investigate spin-coated cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) as a scalable encapsulant for TMDs. Room-temperature and cryogenic optical spectroscopy reveal enhanced photoluminescence and second-harmonic generation, accompanied by excitonic linewidth narrowing and an increased exciton-to-trion ratio. In addition, COC encapsulation induces an excitonic peak splitting and an overall spectral blueshift. First-principles calculations attribute these spectral modifications to local symmetry breaking at the chalcogen interface and macroscopic compressive strain, respectively. These findings establish spin-coated COC as an effective, scalable encapsulation strategy and a potential platform for post-growth excitonic and band-structure engineering.

The spectral changes (peak splitting and blueshift) are attributed to local symmetry breaking at the chalcogen interface and macroscopic compressive strain, respectively, based on first-principles calculations.

However, their optical performance is degraded by environmental exposure and substrate-induced charge trapping, motivating the development of scalable encapsulation strategies.

title: Symmetry-Induced Weyl Nodes in Interacting Multi-Terminal Josephson Junctions
summary: We show that an emergent geometric symmetry generates non-trivial topology in quantum-dot-based multi-terminal Josephson junctions. It confines same-spin Andreev bound state crossings to an analytic one-dimensional manifold of the synthetic Brillouin zone, where interdot coupling selects Weyl nodes of charge $\pm1$ in the singlet sector and doubly degenerate cones of charge $\pm2$ in the doublet sector, at gate-tunable locations. The mechanism yields a spectroscopic detection protocol and a design principle for fabricating devices with non-trivial topological signatures.

AI.tldr: An emergent geometric symmetry in quantum-dot-based multi-terminal Josephson junctions generates non-trivial topology, confining same-spin Andreev bound state crossings to a one-dimensional manifold where Weyl nodes (charge ±1) and doubly degenerate cones (charge ±2) emerge at gate-tunable locations, providing a spectroscopic detection protocol and device design principle.
AI.motivation: To establish a mechanism by which non-trivial topological signatures can emerge in quantum-dot-based multi-terminal Josephson junctions, and to provide both a detection protocol and design guidelines for fabricating devices with such topology.
AI.method: The work leverages an emergent geometric symmetry that restricts same-spin Andreev bound state crossings to an analytic one-dimensional manifold within the synthetic Brillouin zone. Interdot coupling is shown to select Weyl nodes of charge ±1 in the singlet sector and doubly degenerate cones of charge ±2 in the doublet sector, with positions tunable via gate voltages.

AI.conclusion: Emergent geometric symmetry in quantum-dot Josephson junctions provides a controlled route to non-trivial topology, yielding practical spectroscopic detection and device design strategies.

title: The Continuum Model for Uniaxially Strained Bilayer Graphene Moiré Systems
summary: We construct a continuum model for a one-dimensional moiré superlattice formed by stretching one layer of AB-stacked bilayer graphene along the x direction by a factor s. Following the spirit of the Bistritzer-MacDonald model for twisted bilayer graphene, we treat the interlayer coupling as hopping between several Dirac points. At a critical stretch factor s ~ 1.018 the two bands near the Fermi level touch, forming two degeneracy points along the k_y direction. This gap closing is accompanied by a topological phase transition, in which the Chern number changes from 1 to -1, and by a sign change of the Berry-curvature dipole, which we propose can be detected through the nonlinear Hall effect. We find that uniaxial strain modulates inter-Dirac-valley coupling, which drives band gap collapse and subsequent topological number inversion. This opens a route to engineer topological transport and quantum anomalous Hall effects via strain engineering of moiré heterostructures.

At a critical stretch factor of ~1.018, a topological phase transition occurs where the Chern number flips from 1 to -1, accompanied by a Berry-curvature dipole sign change detectable via the nonlinear Hall effect, opening a route to strain-engineered topological transport.
AI.motivation: To explore strain engineering as a novel knob for tuning topological properties in moiré heterostructures, specifically by constructing a tractable continuum model for a one-dimensional moiré superlattice in bilayer graphene that enables systematic study of band structure and topological transitions.
AI.method: The authors construct a continuum model for a 1D moiré superlattice created by stretching one layer of AB-stacked bilayer graphene along x by factor s. Following the Bistritzer-MacDonald approach for twisted bilayer graphene, interlayer coupling is treated as hopping between multiple Dirac points. The model analyzes band structure, Chern numbers, and Berry curvature as functions of strain factor s.

title: Identification of the length scale parameter of simplified strain gradient elasticity from standard Mode I fracture tests
summary: Recently, it was shown that additional material constants of strain gradient elasticity (SGE) can be identified for brittle and quasi-brittle materials based on the analysis of experimental data on the crack size effect. In the present paper, we perform precise numerical simulations within SGE and derive regression relations for processing experimental data from standard fracture mechanics tests under pure Mode I loading conditions (CCT, SENT, SENB). We consider the simplified SGE, whose constitutive relations contain a single length scale parameter $\ell$ in addition to the classical elastic constants. We show that, for brittle materials, this parameter can be explicitly identified as $\ell \approx 0.362 (K_{Ic}/σ_{ult})^2$. This identification ensures that the fracture loads predicted by classical linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) and by the simplified SGE coincide for relatively long Mode I cracks. However, within the simplified SGE, these fracture loads are evaluated from the nonsingular stress field using the maximum principal stress criterion. For quasi-brittle materials, we derive regression relations that describe the non-classical size effect on strength. This effect is usually treated within nonlinear fracture mechanics but can be naturally captured by SGE. Examples of identification of the length scale parameter $\ell$ based on the established relations and the experimental data for chopped fiber composites and for porous and dense quasi-brittle ceramics are presented.

AI.tldr: The paper presents numerical simulations within simplified strain gradient elasticity (SGE) to derive regression relations for identifying a single length scale parameter ℓ from standard Mode I fracture tests (CCT, SENT, SENB). For brittle materials, ℓ ≈ 0.362(K_Ic/σ_ult)² is explicitly identified, ensuring fracture loads coincide with classical LEFM for long cracks. For quasi-brittle materials, regression relations capturing the non-classical size effect on strength are derived and validated against experimental data for chopped fiber composites and porous/dense ceramics.
AI.motivation: To enable identification of additional material constants in strain gradient elasticity (SGE) from standard experimental fracture tests, since previous work showed these constants can be determined from crack size effect data but lacked precise numerical regression relations for practical implementation.
AI.method: The authors perform precise numerical simulations within simplified SGE (containing a single length scale parameter ℓ plus classical elastic constants) and derive regression relations for processing experimental data from standard Mode I fracture mechanics tests (CCT, SENT, SENB). For brittle materials, the length scale parameter is identified via an explicit analytical relation; for quasi-brittle materials, regression relations describe the non-classical size effect, with maximum principal stress criterion applied to the nonsingular stress field.
AI.result: For brittle materials, the length scale parameter is explicitly identified as ℓ ≈ 0.362(K_Ic/σ_ult)², ensuring fracture loads from classical LEFM and simplified SGE coincide for relatively long Mode I cracks. For quasi-brittle materials, regression relations capturing the non-classical size effect on strength are derived. The methodology is demonstrated through identification of ℓ from experimental data for chopped fiber composites and porous and dense quasi-brittle ceramics.
AI.conclusion: Strain gradient elasticity can naturally capture the non-classical size effect on strength typically treated within nonlinear fracture mechanics, and the derived regression relations provide a practical procedure for identifying the length scale parameter ℓ from standard fracture tests on brittle and quasi-brittle materials.

title: Soft and chiral phonons in chiral phase of K3NiO2
summary: Raman scattering measurements confirmed the theoretical prediction that the structural phase transition from the achiral tetragonal to the chiral tetragonal phase, which occurs near 400 K, is induced by a doubly degenerate soft phonon at the Z point of the Brillouin zone. In the low-temperature chiral phase, the soft mode activates in Raman spectra, splits into two components with A1 and B1 symmetries and harden with cooling according to Cochran law. Circularly polarized Raman scattering did not reveal the angular momentum of these singly degenerate phonons at the Gamma point, which is consistent with theory. We also calculated the phonon branches in the whole Brillouin zone for both crystalline phases and compared the results with the phonons observable in the Raman spectra. The calculations revealed that some phonons with nonzero k have angular momentum in the chiral phase. A pronounced circular motion of atoms can be observed, for example, in a Dirac-type topological phonon at the M-point of the Brillouin zone with a frequency of 168 cm-1.

AI.tldr: This paper combines Raman scattering measurements and DFT phonon calculations to confirm that a structural phase transition near 400 K from an achiral to a chiral tetragonal phase is driven by a doubly degenerate soft phonon at the Z point. In the low-temperature chiral phase, the soft mode activates, splits into A1 and B1 components, and hardens per the Cochran law. Circularly polarized Raman scattering found no angular momentum for Gamma-point phonons, but calculations revealed that some phonons with nonzero k (e.g., a Dirac-type topological phonon at the M point at 168 cm-1) exhibit angular momentum with pronounced circular atomic motion.
AI.motivation: To experimentally verify the theoretical prediction of a soft-phonon-driven structural phase transition between achiral and chiral tetragonal phases and to investigate the phonon angular momentum properties in the chiral phase.
AI.method: Raman scattering measurements (including circularly polarized Raman) in both achiral and chiral tetragonal phases, combined with first-principles phonon calculations across the entire Brillouin zone for both phases, with comparison to experimentally observable phonons.
AI.result: Confirmed the doubly degenerate soft phonon at the Z point drives the phase transition near 400 K. The soft mode activates in the chiral phase, splits into A1 and B1 components, and follows the Cochran hardening law. Circularly polarized Raman showed no angular momentum for Gamma-point singly degenerate phonons, consistent with theory. However, calculations identified nonzero-k phonons carrying angular momentum, notably a Dirac-type topological phonon at the M point (168 cm-1) with pronounced circular atomic motion.
AI.conclusion: The phase transition is soft-phonon-driven and the chiral phase hosts phonons with nonzero angular momentum at finite wavevectors, including topological (Dirac-type) phonons, even though Gamma-point phonons carry no angular momentum.

title: Sulfur-rich Spirofluorene-Bridged N Heterotriangulene Redox-Active Polymers
summary: Sulfur-rich spirofluorene-bridged N-heterotriangulene (FTN) polymers featuring covalently linked oligosulfide units and a terthiophene-based analogue were synthesized via nucleophilic aromatic substitution and Stille cross-coupling polymerization. The resulting materials are amorphous, insoluble solids with high thermal stability and sulfur contents up to 25 wt%. Structural and compositional analyses by combustion analysis, ToF-SIMS, FT-IR, XPS, and solid-state NMR confirm the efficient incorporation of short oligosulfide to disulfide linkages and well-defined terthiophene units in the respective polymers. Electrochemical characterization in lithium half-cells reveals a reversible, high-voltage oxidation of the FTN unit at 3.8-4.0 V (vs. Li/Li+), accompanied by low-voltage sulfur- or terthiophene-based redox processes between 1.5-2.5 V (vs. Li/Li+). Sulfur incorporation markedly increases the theoretical and initial discharge capacities (up to 129 mA h g-1), while the sulfide conversion processes exhibit rapid fading and poor reversibility due to sulfide dissolution. In contrast, the terthiophene-linked polymer shows only transient low-voltage activity while maintaining high Coulombic efficiencies (ca. 99.7%) governed by the persistent FTN backbone redox event. Our results highlight how different redox-active linkers influence the electrochemical behavior of FTN-based polymers and provide insights into the design of functional organic cathode materials featuring multi-redox processes.

AI.tldr: Sulfur-rich spirofluorene-bridged N-heterotriangulene (FTN) polymers with oligosulfide and terthiophene linkers were synthesized and evaluated as organic cathode materials. Sulfide-linked polymers show high capacities (up to 129 mA h g-1) but poor reversibility due to sulfide dissolution, while the terthiophene-linked polymer exhibits stable FTN backbone redox with ~99.7% Coulombic efficiency.
AI.motivation: To investigate how different redox-active linker units (oligosulfides vs. terthiophene) influence the electrochemical behavior of N-heterotriangulene-based polymers, with the goal of understanding the design principles for functional organic cathode materials featuring multi-redox processes.
AI.method: FTN polymers with oligosulfide linkers were synthesized via nucleophilic aromatic substitution, while a terthiophene-linked analogue was made via Stille cross-coupling polymerization. Materials were characterized by combustion analysis, ToF-SIMS, FT-IR, XPS, and solid-state NMR, then evaluated electrochemically in lithium half-cells.
AI.result: Polymers were amorphous, insoluble, thermally stable solids with sulfur contents up to 25 wt%. The FTN unit exhibited reversible high-voltage oxidation at 3.8-4.0 V vs. Li/Li+, while sulfur/terthiophene redox occurred at 1.5-2.5 V. Sulfur incorporation raised discharge capacity to 129 mA h g-1 but suffered rapid fading from sulfide dissolution; the terthiophene polymer showed transient low-voltage activity with ~99.7% Coulombic efficiency governed by persistent FTN backbone redox.
AI.conclusion: Different redox-active linkers drastically affect the electrochemical behavior of FTN-based polymers: sulfide linkers boost capacity but sacrifice reversibility, whereas terthiophene linkers preserve cycling stability through the persistent FTN backbone redox. title: Symmetry-engineering ferroelectricity in silicon dioxides
summary: It is a long-established rule for classical ferroelectricity that any ferroelectric crystal must adopt one of the 10 specific polar point groups. Here we predict a unique type of ferroelectricity that can be generated in some crystals belonging to nonpolar noncentrosymmetric groups. This principle can be applicable to many systems including silicon dioxides, the most widely used dielectric materials. Most of their crystalline phases do not belong the polar groups, while the nonlinear Si-O-Si configurations lead to multiple identical states. We show first-principles evidence that the crystal symmetry forbidding the formation of polarizations, can be broken by either parallel surfaces in thin-films or applying a uniaxial strain. As a result, the multiple identical states are endowed with polarizations of different directions, and low-barrier ferroelectric switching can be realized via transition between them, which can be room-temperature robust down to the thickness of 1 nm. Our findings may not only enable low-cost and large-scale manufacture of ferroelectrics directly integrated in silicon chips, but also open a new avenue for exploring ferroelectricity in prevalent nonpolar materials.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts a new type of ferroelectricity that can arise in crystals belonging to nonpolar noncentrosymmetric point groups, contrary to the classical rule that ferroelectricity requires one of 10 polar point groups. Using first-principles calculations on silicon dioxides, the authors show that symmetry breaking via thin-film surfaces or uniaxial strain can induce polarization with multiple identical states, enabling low-barrier ferroelectric switching that is room-temperature robust down to 1 nm thickness.
AI.motivation: To challenge the classical ferroelectricity paradigm that restricts it to 10 polar point groups, and to extend ferroelectricity to ubiquitous nonpolar materials such as silicon dioxide, enabling low-cost integration with silicon chip technology.
AI.method: The authors use first-principles calculations to demonstrate that in crystals belonging to nonpolar noncentrosymmetric groups (e.g., silicon dioxides), symmetry that forbids polarization can be broken by either parallel surfaces in thin films or applying uniaxial strain, thereby generating multiple identical states with different polarization directions.
AI.result: The proposed mechanism enables low-barrier ferroelectric switching via transitions between the multiple identical states, and the ferroelectricity remains robust at room temperature down to a thickness of 1 nm.
AI.conclusion: This work not only enables low-cost, large-scale manufacture of ferroelectrics directly integrated into silicon chips, but also opens a new avenue for exploring ferroelectricity in prevalent nonpolar materials.

title: Chemical Control of Electronic Structure and Topology in Tellurium-Encapsulated Silicene
summary: We investigate chemical control of the electronic, optical, and topological properties of two-dimensional \ce{Si2X2Te2} (\ce{X} = \ce{B}, \ce{Al}, \ce{Ga}, and \ce{In}) monolayers using first-principles calculations. All compounds are dynamically stable semiconductors, with their vibrational and electronic properties evolving systematically upon group-III substitution. Hybrid-functional calculations including spin--orbit coupling reveal predominantly $p$-orbital band edges and increasingly pronounced relativistic effects from B to In. Most notably, the calculated $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant identifies \ce{Si2In2Te2} as a candidate quantum spin Hall insulator, while the B-, Al-, and Ga-based monolayers remain topologically trivial. Bethe--Salpeter calculations further show that electron--hole interactions redistribute oscillator strength near the absorption onset while preserving a weak in-plane optical anisotropy. Our results establish group-III substitution as a simple chemical route to tune the electronic structure and drive a transition from trivial to nontrivial topology in \ce{Si2X2Te2} monolayers.

AI.tldr: First-principles study shows group-III substitution (B, Al, Ga, In) systematically tunes electronic, optical, and topological properties of Si2X2Te2 monolayers, with Si2In2Te2 emerging as a candidate quantum spin Hall insulator while lighter-III analogues remain topologically trivial.
AI.motivation: To explore a simple chemical route—group-III substitution—for controlling the electronic structure and inducing a topological transition in two-dimensional Si2X2Te2 monolayers.
AI.method: First-principles calculations with hybrid functionals including spin–orbit coupling for electronic structure and Z2 invariants; Bethe–Salpeter calculations for optical properties including electron–hole interactions.
AI.result: All monolayers are dynamically stable semiconductors with systematic evolution of vibrational/electronic properties from B to In. Z2 invariants identify Si2In2Te2 as a candidate quantum spin Hall insulator, while B/Al/Ga analogues are topologically trivial. Bethe–Salpeter results show electron–hole interactions redistribute oscillator strength near the absorption onset while preserving weak in-plane optical anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: Group-III substitution provides a simple chemical route to tune electronic structure and drive a transition from trivial to nontrivial topology in Si2X2Te2 monolayers.

title: Dirac Surface States and Nonlocal Quantum Tunneling in Topological Semiconductor Mo$_2$SeTe$_3$ for High-Performance Tunnel FETs
summary: A first-principles and device-level study of the quasi-two-dimensional transition-metal chalcogenide Mo$_2$SeTe$_3$ is performed. The material is found to be a weak topological semiconductor with a finite bulk band gap and symmetry-protected Dirac surface states, indicating strong potential for next-generation low-power quantum electronic devices. An SOC-driven band inversion accompanied by an indirect semiconducting gap of approximately 0.75 eV is observed. Topological nontriviality is rigorously confirmed through Wannier charge-center evolution and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant analysis, yielding weak topological indices of $(0;001)$, while iterative Green's-function surface-state calculations corroborate Dirac-cone conducting states traversing the bulk gap on symmetry-preserving surfaces. Mo$_2$SeTe$_3$ additionally exhibits exceptional dynamical and mechanical stability, pronounced optical anisotropy, high dielectric polarizability, broad infrared-to-visible optical absorption, a large static dielectric constant, and substantial birefringence, making it favorable for photonic and optoelectronic applications. Thermoelectric transport analyses further reveal enhanced carrier mobility and a competitive figure of merit under $n$-type doping near room temperature. A dual-source tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) is implemented via TCAD simulations with nonlocal band-to-band tunneling, yielding subthreshold switching below the thermionic limit, a high ON/OFF current ratio, and enhanced tunneling efficiency driven by SOC-induced orbital hybridization and topologically enhanced interband coupling. The concurrent realization of nontrivial bulk-boundary correspondence, robust transport properties, and steep-slope switching characteristics establishes Mo$_2$SeTe$_3$ as a multifunctional quantum material platform for topological and next-generation energy-efficient nanoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: A combined first-principles and device-level study investigates the quasi-2D transition-metal chalcogenide Mo₂SeTe₃, revealing it as a weak topological semiconductor with a ~0.75 eV band gap, symmetry-protected Dirac surface states, topological indices (0;001), and exceptional optical, thermoelectric, and mechanical properties. A dual-source TFET realized via TCAD simulations achieves subthermionic switching with high ON/OFF ratios, establishing Mo₂SeTe₃ as a multifunctional quantum material platform.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to identify a quasi-two-dimensional material that simultaneously possesses topological nontriviality and robust device-level performance, addressing the need for next-generation low-power quantum electronic and photonic devices.
AI.method: The study employs first-principles density functional theory calculations (including SOC), Wannier charge-center evolution, Z₂ invariant analysis, iterative Green's-function surface-state simulations, and TCAD device simulations with nonlocal band-to-band tunneling for a dual-source tunnel field-effect transistor.
AI.result: Mo₂SeTe₃ is confirmed as a weak topological semiconductor with indirect band gap ~0.75 eV, topological indices (0;001), and Dirac-cone surface states. It exhibits dynamical/mechanical stability, optical anisotropy, broad infrared-to-visible absorption, large static dielectric constant, birefringence, enhanced thermoelectric figure of merit under n-type doping, and subthermionic TFET switching with high ON/OFF ratio.
AI.conclusion: Mo₂SeTe₃ concurrently realizes nontrivial bulk-boundary correspondence, robust transport properties, and steep-slope switching behavior, making it a multifunctional quantum material platform for topological and energy-efficient nanoelectronic devices.
